items.title: How WY2026 inflow forecasts were translated into a two-step cut in Glen Canyon Dam releases
items.operational_question: How did Water Year 2026 inflow forecasts, tier classification, and the 2024 Section 6.E authority combine to produce the 2026 reduction in Lake Powell releases?
items.synthesis_claim: The WY2026 release decision moved through a documented sequence: the August 2025 24-Month Study placed Lake Powell in the Mid-Elevation Release Tier with a projected 7.48 maf release; projections below the 3,525 ft DROA target elevation led Reclamation to reduce December 2025-April 2026 monthly releases by 0.598 maf; and when continued record-low inflow forecasts projected Lake Powell below 3,500 ft, Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 ROD to cut the annual release from 7.48 to 6.00 maf, paired with 0.66-1.0 maf of DROA releases from Flaming Gorge.
items.scope_and_conditions: Water Year 2026 operations of Glen Canyon Dam under the 2007 Interim Guidelines as supplemented by the 2024 Near-term Colorado River Operations SEIS ROD. Section 6.E applies only in the Mid-Elevation Release and Lower Elevation Balancing Tiers and is triggered by the minimum probable 24-Month Study; it sets a floor of 6.0 maf. The 0.598 maf monthly adjustment and the 6.00 maf annual figure are reported in the July 2026 24-Month Study; the 1.48 maf reduction is stated by Reclamation as applying through September 2026.

analysis_chain.statement: CBRFC Ensemble Streamflow Prediction scenarios (probable minimum, most probable, probable maximum) feed the 24-Month Study; by spring-summer 2026 the WY2026 unregulated inflow forecast had fallen to about 3.50 maf (36% of average), with a minimum probable inflow of 2.78 maf (29% of average).

The August 2025 24-Month Study projected a January 1, 2026 Lake Powell elevation below 3,575 ft and at or above 3,525 ft, so the Mid-Elevation Release Tier governed WY2026 with a projected 7.48 maf release.

analysis_chain.stage: first response: protect the DROA target elevation
analysis_chain.statement: The July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell below the 3,525 ft DROA target elevation, triggering drought-response planning; to protect that target, December 2025-April 2026 monthly releases were reduced by 0.598 maf in the December 2025 24-Month Study.

Section 6.E of the 2024 ROD directs that, in the Mid-Elevation Release or Lower Elevation Balancing Tier, if the minimum probable 24-Month Study projects an elevation below 3,500 ft within 12 months, the Secretary begin planning to reduce releases to not less than 6.0 maf to maintain 3,500 ft.

With conditions projected below 3,500 ft, Interior reduced the WY2026 release from 7.48 to 6.00 maf under Section 6.E, in conjunction with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing about 0.66-1.0 maf from Flaming Gorge by April 2027; Reclamation described the combined package as adding up to about 2.48 maf to Lake Powell.

supporting_evidence.summary: For 2026 operations, three unregulated inflow scenarios were developed using the CBRFC Ensemble Streamflow Prediction model: probable minimum (90% exceedance) at 4.20 maf (44% of average), most probable (50% exceedance) at 7.86 maf (82% of average), and probable maximum (10% exceedance) at 15.17 maf (158% of average) for Lake Powell in water year 2026.

supporting_evidence.summary: The July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study reports the full WY2026 unregulated inflow forecast for Lake Powell as 3.50 maf, 36 percent of the 1991-2020 average (OFF-023-05). The Lower Colorado Weekly Hydrologic Update dated July 27, 2026 reports the WY2026 unregulated inflow forecast as 3,501 kaf (36% of normal), an increase of 10 kaf from the previous forecast of 3,491 kaf (also 36% of normal) (OFF-024-02).

Circle of Blue reporting (April 2026) states inflows into Lake Powell in 2026 are projected to be the lowest ever measured, breaking the previous record set in 2002, driven by a downward snowpack trend and a March 2026 heat wave that was the most extreme on record in the Southwest for that time of year (MED-001-05). Reclamation's newsroom release states Lake Powell's water year 2026 minimum probable inflow is forecasted at just 2.78 million acre-feet, 29 percent of historical average and one of the lowest on record, with Reclamation's April 24-Month Study projecting Lake Powell may decline below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool) by August 2026 without major intervention (OFF-035-01).

Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines' Mid-Elevation Release Tier (Section 6.C), when the projected January 1 Lake Powell elevation is below 3,575 feet and at or above 3,525 feet, the Secretary releases 7.48 maf from Lake Powell in the Water Year if the projected January 1 Lake Mead elevation is at or above 1,025 feet (or 8.23 maf if Lake Mead is below 1,025 feet). Both the Draft 2026 Annual Operating Plan and the July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study confirm this Mid-Elevation Release Tier (per 2007 Interim Guidelines Section 6.C.1 and the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD Section 6.E) governs Lake Powell operations for Water Year 2026, with the August 2025 24-Month Study's most probable inflow scenario originally projecting a 7.48 maf release from Glen Canyon Dam for WY2026.

Under the Upper Basin DCP's DROA, Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above elevation 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool (EU-LP-CRS-001-04). Reclamation's stated operational goal under DROA is to 'protect' this 3,525-ft elevation, primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial-unit reservoirs (EU-LP-CRS-002-04). The DROA establishes the process for Reclamation, in collaboration with the Upper Basin States, to release additional water from upstream CRSP initial-unit reservoirs (Flaming Gorge, Aspinall, Navajo, Glen Canyon/Lake Powell) to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation (EU-LP-OFF-017-03). In CRSS modeling, Powell Infrastructure Protection (PIP) releases from the Upper Initial Units (Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Navajo) are specifically triggered when Lake Powell is projected to fall below elevation 3,525 feet (EU-LP-OFF-021-06). This target was actually invoked when the July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell declining below the 3,525.00-ft DROA target elevation, triggering DROA year-2025 drought-response planning under the DCP-related agreements (EU-LP-OFF-022-03); consistent with protecting this same target, the December 2025 24-Month Study reduced Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes for December 2025 through April 2026 by 0.598 maf (EU-LP-OFF-023-03).

Under the 2024 near-term consensus agreement / 2024 ROD's new Section XI.G.6.E (per CRS summary and the official Record of Decision), if the minimum probable 24-Month Study projects an elevation below 3,500 feet at Lake Powell in the next 12 months, the Secretary must begin planning to reduce Lake Powell releases as needed to not less than 6.0 maf for the Water Year to maintain elevation 3,500 feet -- in lieu of a 7.0 maf figure referenced under the near-term proposal framing.

On April 17, 2026, the Bureau of Reclamation announced unprecedented actions to store more water in Lake Powell -- then less than 25 percent full -- to preserve hydropower generation and protect Glen Canyon Dam water-delivery infrastructure the agency said was at risk from low reservoir levels (EU-LP-MED-001-01). With the consent of the four Upper Basin states, Reclamation committed to releasing between 660,000 and 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (82 percent full) into Lake Powell over the 12 months following the announcement, building on a smaller 463,000-acre-foot release used to prop up Powell in 2022-23 (EU-LP-MED-001-02). Because WY2026 was historically dry and Lake Powell was projected to decline below elevation 3,500 feet, the Department of the Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to reduce Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, coupled with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing approximately 660,000 to 1.00 maf of additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to Lake Powell by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-023-02). Reclamation's newsroom release confirms the combined plan: adding about 2.48 million acre-feet via the 660,000 AF-1 maf Flaming Gorge release (April 2026-April 2027, under the 2019 Drought Response Operating Agreements) plus the 7.48-to-6.0-maf release reduction through September 2026 under Section 6E, together expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation about 54 feet to at least 3,500 feet by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-035-02).

Reclamation's '24-Month Study' is the recurring monthly operational model that projects Colorado River reservoir levels 24 months into the future to inform near-term operating decisions, with each monthly run modeling a single scenario of reservoir conditions. Operationally, projected monthly inflow volumes from probabilistic hydrologic scenarios are input into the 24-Month Study, and the resulting projected monthly releases for each system reservoir are adjusted from the prior month's 24-Month Study baseline until release and storage levels best accomplish project purposes and operational objectives.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The sources do not state which specific monthly 24-Month Study run formally triggered the Section 6.E planning step; the Reclamation news release cites the April 2026 24-Month Study projecting a decline below 3,490 ft by August 2026 without intervention. The statement that this was the first use of Section 6.E comes from a media source (MED-001), not an official document. Forecast values changed month to month (for example 3,491 to 3,501 kaf), so figures are tied to the dated study that reports them.
items.operational_implication: A user asking why the 2026 Glen Canyon Dam release was 6.00 maf rather than the tier volume of 7.48 maf needs the full sequence: tier rule, DROA target protection, the Section 6.E trigger and floor, and the paired upstream releases. No single source states the whole chain.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-023 confirmed the order of actions: 'To protect a target elevation at Lake Powell of 3,525 feet, adjustments to Glen Canyon Dam monthly volume releases for the months of December 2025 through April 2026 ... reducing the release volume for these months by 0.598 maf', followed by 'the Department of the Interior implemented an action under Section 6.E ... by reducing Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf in WY 2026.' Rereading OFF-002 narrowed the trigger to the minimum probable 24-Month Study and a floor of 'not less than 6.0 maf'. OFF-035 states the reduction applies 'through September 2026'. The candidate claim was narrowed to keep the December 2025 DROA-target adjustment as a separate first step rather than part of the Section 6.E action.

items.title: A met sediment trigger is necessary but not sufficient for a High-Flow Experiment
items.operational_question: How is a High-Flow Experiment (HFE) at Glen Canyon Dam decided once a sediment trigger is reached, and what conditions can stop it?
items.synthesis_claim: Under the 2012 protocol and LTEMP, a sediment trigger makes an HFE eligible rather than automatic: the decision is then screened against annual-release-volume limits, reservoir elevation, and other resource conditions. Documented outcomes show these screens are used in practice: fall HFEs were not implemented in 2015, 2021, and 2022 although sediment triggers were met, because of warm release temperatures and nonnative-fish entrainment risk, and the 2024 SEIS changed the sediment accounting so that untriggered or forgone sediment can roll over.
items.scope_and_conditions: HFEs under the 2012 HFE protocol and the 2016 LTEMP ROD (Alternative D), as amended by the 2024 LTEMP SEIS. The extended-duration fall HFE limits (no more than four in 20 years; not implemented if annual release volume would be affected) apply to that HFE type only. The 3,500 ft limit is a modeling assumption stated in the 2024 SEIS, not a codified ROD rule.

analysis_chain.statement: HFEs follow a decision-making protocol approved in 2012 that times dam releases to follow large tributary sand inputs; the protocol defines conditions for implementation and a method for setting timing, magnitude, and duration.

HFEs change only monthly and hourly release patterns while annual volumes continue to comply with the LROC as implemented through the 2007 Interim Guidelines; an extended-duration fall HFE will not be implemented if annual release volume would be affected, and no more than four are allowed over the 20-year LTEMP period.

The 2024 SEIS assumes no HFE below Lake Powell elevation 3,500 ft, because achievable magnitude would fall below 37,000 cfs and a release could increase the risk of dropping below the 3,490 ft power pool.

The Department decided not to implement fall HFEs in 2015, 2021, and 2022 despite reaching sediment input triggers, citing increased water temperatures and higher potential for entrainment of warmwater nonnative fish.

Traditionally Associated Tribes must be notified at least 30 days before planned experimental flows including HFEs; the 2024 SEIS replaced the semiannual sediment accounting period with an annual period allowing a spring or fall HFE, or both, with rollover of sediment when a trigger is met but no HFE is implemented.

supporting_evidence.summary: High-flow experiments (HFEs) — short-duration controlled floods released from Glen Canyon Dam to rebuild sandbars — are conducted under a decision-making protocol approved by the Department of the Interior in 2012 that coordinates dam releases to occur following large sand inputs delivered to the Colorado River by a major tributary.

supporting_evidence.summary: High flow experiments were tested in 1996, 1997, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2013, and 2014 to rebuild eroded sandbars; since 2012 a 10-year protocol implements one to two high flow experiments annually, timed to follow tributary sand inputs from the Paria River in fall and/or spring (EU-LP-RES-014-05). This decision-making protocol, approved by the Department of the Interior in 2012, coordinates dam releases to occur following large sand inputs delivered to the Colorado River by a major tributary (EU-LP-RES-018-01). Across the full historical record, 11 HFEs were released from Glen Canyon Dam between 1996 and November 2018, with peak magnitudes ranging from 864 to 1,274 cubic meters per second and durations from 24 to 168 hours, including lower-magnitude habitat maintenance flows (HMFs) in 1997 and 2000 (EU-LP-RES-018-02).

High-Flow Experiment (HFE) releases from Glen Canyon Dam are triggered when there is sufficient sediment input from the Paria River and typically range from approximately 30,000 to 45,000 cfs, used to mobilize channel-stored sand and redeposit it as sandbars, beaches, and associated backwater/riparian habitat. An HFE is defined as using full powerplant capacity (30,000 cfs) plus the four bypass (river outlet) tubes (15,000 cfs), for a combined magnitude up to about 45,000 cfs depending on the number of functional generators/penstocks, with release durations of about 2 to 7 days. Most HFEs are limited to a maximum duration of 96 hours under the 2011 HFE protocol, though some LTEMP alternatives allow extended-duration HFEs when adequate sediment supply is available.

Under LTEMP Alternative D, extended-duration fall HFEs (greater than 96 hours) are capped at no more than four occurrences over the 20-year LTEMP period, triggered by the modeled sand mass balance from Paria River sediment inputs during the defined fall accounting period (July 1-November 30). However, an extended-duration HFE will not be implemented if doing so would affect the annual release volume -- meaning the legal requirement to meet the annual release volume can override an otherwise-triggered extended-duration fall HFE.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The evidence documents the 2015, 2021, and 2022 non-implementation decisions and their stated reasons, but not the full list of years in which triggers were met, so the frequency of forgone HFEs cannot be computed here. The source text for EU-LP-OFF-006-12 reads 'sediment or hydrology triggers', not only sediment triggers as the EU quote states; this card relies on the source wording.
items.operational_implication: A sediment-trigger signal should not be read as a prediction that an HFE will occur. Whether an HFE happens depends on annual volume, elevation, and temperature or nonnative-fish conditions that are recorded in different documents.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-007 confirmed: 'there have been years in which sediment conditions warranted a recommendation for an HFE release, but an HFE release was not implemented based on other resource conditions. The Department made the decision not to implement fall HFE releases in 2015, 2021, and 2022 ...'. OFF-003 confirms 'Water delivery issues will be considered before deciding to implement an extended-duration fall HFE. An extended-duration HFE will not be implemented if annual release volume would be affected.' Rereading OFF-006 showed the original wording is 'triggered based upon sediment or hydrology triggers', which is broader than the EU-LP-OFF-006-12 quote; the card was worded to avoid claiming that sediment is the only trigger.

items.title: The annual Lake Powell release is set once a year and then recomputed monthly
items.operational_question: Through what process is Lake Powell's annual release volume determined and adjusted during a water year?
items.synthesis_claim: The annual release is not a single fixed decision. The LROC is implemented each year through the Annual Operating Plan (AOP) using the 2007 Interim Guidelines; the 24-Month Study projects storage and sets the operating tier from the projected end-of-calendar-year (January 1) Lake Powell elevation; and in the Equalization and Balancing Tiers the scheduled water-year release is adjusted each month as inflow forecasts and projected September 30 storage change. Basin States are given the 24-Month Study assumptions before the April and August studies that drive these adjustments.
items.scope_and_conditions: Annual release determination for Glen Canyon Dam under the LROC, the 2007 Interim Guidelines (through 2026), and the 2019 DCP Companion Agreement. Monthly adjustment as described here applies in the Equalization, Upper Elevation Balancing, and Lower Elevation Balancing Tiers; the Mid-Elevation Release Tier specifies a fixed volume (7.48 maf) subject to later rules such as Section 6.E. The January-July monthly recomputation description comes from a 1996 GAO report and predates the 2007 tiers.

analysis_chain.statement: The Interim Guidelines are used each year to implement the LROC through issuance of the AOP, which section 602(b) of the 1968 Colorado River Basin Project Act requires as a single integrated reference on past and anticipated operations.

Projected monthly inflows are entered into the 24-Month Study, starting from projected storage conditions, and releases are adjusted to accomplish project purposes; in CRSS the operating tier is set in January from the end-of-calendar-year Lake Powell elevation (for example, 3,525-3,575 ft gives the Mid-Elevation Release Tier).

Equalization releases require Lake Powell above the elevation in the Equalization Elevation Table, with the 2004 interim 602(a) storage guideline setting 3,630 ft (about 14.85 maf); if that elevation is reached and Lake Mead is projected below 1,105 ft on September 30, additional water is released to Lake Mead.

In the Equalization and Balancing Tiers, scheduled water-year releases are adjusted each month based on forecast inflow and projected September 30 active storage at both reservoirs; the 1996 GAO description of practice likewise states that the remaining-year volume is recomputed each month of the January-July forecast season.

Under the DCP Companion Agreement the Secretary must describe 24-Month Study assumptions and projected operations to the Basin States Parties before completing the April and August studies, and under LTEMP Reclamation holds monthly Glen Canyon Dam operational coordination meetings with DOI bureaus, WAPA, and Basin State liaisons.

supporting_evidence.summary: The Interim Guidelines are implemented by the Secretary each year through the Criteria for Coordinated Long-Range Operation of Colorado River Reservoirs (established pursuant to the Colorado River Basin Project Act of 1968), issued via the Annual Operating Plan, and would remain in effect for determinations made through 2025 regarding operations through 2026.

supporting_evidence.summary: The 2007 Interim Guidelines are implemented annually by the Secretary through the Criteria for Coordinated Long-Range Operation of Colorado River Reservoirs (LROC), established pursuant to the Colorado River Basin Project Act (CRBPA) of September 30, 1968, and issued via the Annual Operating Plan (AOP). The AOP itself is the single, integrated reference document required by Section 602(b) of the CRBPA of 1968, and it memorializes operational decisions made under multiple individual federal actions, including the Interim Surplus Guidelines, the 1996 Glen Canyon Dam ROD, and the 2007 Interim Guidelines.

Reclamation's '24-Month Study' is the recurring monthly operational model that projects Colorado River reservoir levels 24 months into the future to inform near-term operating decisions, with each monthly run modeling a single scenario of reservoir conditions. Operationally, projected monthly inflow volumes from probabilistic hydrologic scenarios are input into the 24-Month Study, and the resulting projected monthly releases for each system reservoir are adjusted from the prior month's 24-Month Study baseline until release and storage levels best accomplish project purposes and operational objectives.

The Interim Guidelines for Coordinated Operations of Lake Powell and Lake Mead define four operating tiers -- the Equalization Tier, Upper Elevation Balancing Tier, Mid-Elevation Release Tier, and Lower Elevation Balancing Tier -- with scheduled Lake Powell water-year releases adjusted each month based on forecast inflow and projected September 30 elevations at both reservoirs. In CRSS modeling of the Continued Current Strategies baseline, each January's governing tier is set by end-of-calendar-year pool elevation: the Equalization Tier applies at or above the Equalization Level; the Upper Elevation Balancing Tier applies down to elevation 3,575 feet; the Mid-Elevation Release Tier applies between 3,575 and 3,525 feet; and the Lower Elevation Balancing Tier applies below elevation 3,525 feet.

Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines Section 6.A (Equalization Tier), if Lake Powell reaches the elevation stated in the Lake Powell Equalization Elevation Table for a given Water Year and the September 30 projected Lake Mead elevation is below 1,105 feet, the Secretary releases additional water from Lake Powell to Lake Mead until the reservoirs fully equalize, Lake Mead reaches 1,105 feet, or Lake Powell reaches 20 feet below its equalization elevation. Reclamation's 2004 interim 602(a) storage guideline, in effect through 2026, supplies the concrete current value implementing this mechanism: Lake Powell's elevation must be above 3,630 feet (approximately 14.85 maf of storage) for equalization releases between Lake Powell and Lake Mead to occur at all.

The 2007 Biological Assessment on Experimental Releases from Glen Canyon Dam states that when Lake Powell and Lake Mead operations are in the equalization tier, upper elevation balancing tier, or lower elevation balancing tier under the 2007 Shortage ROD, scheduled Lake Powell water-year releases are adjusted each month based on forecasted inflow and projected September 30 active storage at both Lake Powell and Lake Mead (OFF-011-05). The 2008 Final Biological Opinion for Glen Canyon Dam operations restates the same rule in nearly identical language, per the Shortage Guidelines ROD, and additionally notes that releases greater than 9.5 maf generally occur during equalization of storage contents between the two reservoirs (OFF-012-05).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The monthly-recomputation description in OFF-010 reflects practice before the 2007 Interim Guidelines; the evidence set does not state whether Mid-Elevation Release Tier volumes are revised monthly other than through specific provisions such as Section 6.E. CRSS modeling logic (OFF-021) describes how the model represents the rule, which may simplify the administrative process.
items.operational_implication: A release figure quoted from an AOP or an early 24-Month Study is a projection that can change during the year; any question about 'the' annual release needs the date of the study and the tier in force.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-011 and OFF-012 confirmed the monthly-adjustment rule is limited to 'the equalization tier, the upper elevation balancing tier, or the lower elevation balancing tier' and is 'based on forecasted inflow and projected September 30 active storage'. OFF-010 was confirmed as describing pre-2007 practice ('Each month during the inflow forecast season (January to July), the volume of water to be released for the rest of the year is recomputed'). OFF-021 shows CRSS sets the tier from the end-of-calendar-year elevation. The candidate claim was narrowed so that monthly adjustment is not attributed to the Mid-Elevation Release Tier.

items.title: Population thresholds trigger an escalating sequence of humpback chub and trout actions under LTEMP
items.operational_question: How do monitored fish population estimates translate into flow and non-flow actions for humpback chub and rainbow trout below Glen Canyon Dam?
items.synthesis_claim: LTEMP and the 2008 Biological Opinion define a threshold-based escalation tied to the currently accepted humpback chub population model. If the combined adult estimate for the Little Colorado River aggregation falls below 9,000 (2,000 mainstem and 7,000 in the Little Colorado River), Tier 1 conservation actions for rearing and recruitment are implemented. If those do not halt a decline and the adult estimate falls below 7,000, Tier 2 mechanical removal of nonnative fish begins, with up to six monthly trips, and stops when a predator index or recovery criteria are met. Separately, Trout Management Flows, a flow action of high releases followed by a rapid drop to 5,000-8,000 cfs, are triggered by predicted high young-of-year trout recruitment. A drop below 3,500 adults in any year was set in 2008 as a trigger for reinitiating ESA consultation.
items.scope_and_conditions: LTEMP Alternative D (2016 ROD) and the 2008 Biological Opinion reinitiation trigger. Thresholds are point estimates from the population model current at the time of decision; the 2008 trigger uses the ASMR model within its 95% confidence interval. Of these actions, only TMFs change dam releases; Tier 1 and Tier 2 are non-flow actions.

analysis_chain.statement: Adult (>=200 mm) humpback chub numbers are estimated with the currently accepted population model; young-of-year trout recruitment is predicted for the trout trigger.

Tier 1 conservation actions are implemented if the combined adult estimate for the mainstem Little Colorado River aggregation and the Little Colorado River falls below 9,000 (2,000 mainstem, 7,000 tributary).

If Tier 1 actions do not halt the decline and the adult estimate falls below 7,000, up to six monthly mechanical-removal trips are made each triggered year; removal stops when the predator index is below 60 rainbow trout/km for at least 2 years with low immigration, or when adult chub exceed 7,500 and subadult recruitment exceeds adult mortality for at least 2 years.

TMFs, triggered by predicted high young-of-year trout recruitment regardless of cause, use repeated cycles of sustained high flows (for example 20,000 cfs for 2 days to 1 week) followed by a rapid drop to 5,000-8,000 cfs.

Reclamation and FWS defined a reinitiation-of-consultation trigger if the adult population declines significantly or, in any single year, drops below 3,500 adults within the 95% confidence interval of the ASMR model.

items.title: Adaptive management advises; the Secretary of the Interior decides
items.operational_question: Who decides how Glen Canyon Dam operations and experiments are carried out, and what roles do the adaptive management program and decision analysis play?
items.synthesis_claim: Authority over Glen Canyon Dam sub-annual operations and experiments rests with the Secretary of the Interior, while the surrounding institutions are advisory. The Adaptive Management Work Group, a federal advisory committee of agencies, Basin States, Tribes, power customers, and environmental and recreation groups, evaluates dam operations and recommends changes; the LTEMP ROD states that the Secretary retains sole discretion to decide how to accomplish operations and experiments each year. In selecting LTEMP, structured decision analysis informed but did not determine the preferred alternative, and DOI chose the term 'decision analysis' specifically because the Secretary retains decision authority.
items.scope_and_conditions: Governance of Glen Canyon Dam operations under the Grand Canyon Protection Act and the LTEMP ROD. Annual release volumes are set under the LROC and Interim Guidelines, which have their own consultation processes with Basin States and are not decided through the AMWG.

analysis_chain.statement: The Adaptive Management Program is a federal advisory committee that evaluates the performance of dam operations and non-flow treatments using monitoring and research and makes recommendations to DOI; its work group includes federal and state agencies, the seven Basin States, Tribes, hydropower contractors, and environmental, conservation, and recreation groups.
The Secretary of the Interior retains sole discretion to decide how best to accomplish operations and experiments in any given year pursuant to the ROD and other binding obligations.

Structured decision analysis informed the joint leads' analysis but was not the only method used to identify the preferred alternative; DOI used the term 'decision analysis' because the Secretary retains responsibility and authority to decide.

Reclamation seeks consensus on the annual hydrograph through monthly operational coordination calls and regular GCDAMP technical and work group meetings, and must notify Traditionally Associated Tribes at least 30 days before planned experimental flows.

Its formal structure comprises the Secretary's Designee, the Adaptive Management Work Group (AMWG), the Technical Work Group, the Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center, and Independent Review Panels, funded by Reclamation at approximately $8 million annually from power revenues. Critically, the Secretary of the Interior retains sole discretion to decide how best to accomplish dam operations and experiments in any given year; AMWG functions only in an advisory capacity.

The Glen Canyon Dam Adaptive Management Work Group (AMWG), established in 1997 under the GCDAMP, is a federal advisory committee whose membership includes federal and state resource management agencies, representatives of the seven basin states, American Indian Tribes, hydroelectric power purchase contractors, and environmental/conservation and recreational interest groups (EU-LP-OFF-004-06). Its duties are in an advisory capacity only (EU-LP-OFF-011-12); its recommendations for adjustments to Glen Canyon Dam operations under the Grand Canyon Protection Act are conveyed to the Secretary of the Interior (EU-LP-OFF-012-16).

Instead, the preferred alternative was based on the full EIS analysis together with public comment, socioeconomic considerations, and AMWG stakeholder input, with SDA/decision-analysis outputs serving as an appendix to the Draft and Final EIS that informed, but did not replace, the Secretary's decision.

items.title: Below minimum power pool, physical capacity, cavitation limits, and outlet reliability jointly cap Glen Canyon Dam releases
items.operational_question: What constraints determine how much water Glen Canyon Dam can release if Lake Powell falls below minimum power pool (3,490 ft)?
items.synthesis_claim: Below 3,490 ft the penstocks can no longer pass water and all releases must go through the four river outlet works tubes. Three constraints then stack: design capacity that falls with head (15,000 cfs at 3,490 ft; an estimated 10,200 cfs, about 7.41 maf/yr, at 3,430 ft, below the 8.23 maf LROC objective); interim per-conduit flow limits set to reduce cavitation damage; and Reclamation's 2024 conclusion that the outlet works should not be relied on as the sole release path. Because significant structural alterations would require congressional authorization, the operating response has been to keep Lake Powell above 3,490 ft, which places the burden on release reductions.
items.scope_and_conditions: Glen Canyon Dam low-elevation operations as documented from the original design paper (1960s) through the March 2024 Interim Operating Guidance, the 2024 LTEMP SEIS, and the 2025 Post-2026 alternatives report. The 3,430 ft / 10,200 cfs figure is a single study cited by CRS, not a Reclamation operating rule. Elevations in OFF-025 are NGVD29.

analysis_chain.statement: Minimum water surface for power operation is 3,490 ft; below it water cannot be released through the penstocks and must pass through the river outlet works, which the dam was not envisioned to rely on.

The outlets were designed for 15,000 cfs at 3,490 ft (3,750 cfs per tube); one study estimated only 10,200 cfs (7.41 maf/yr) at 3,430 ft, less than the 8.23 maf/yr requirement, and post-2026 alternatives state that releases may be less than specified below 3,490 ft because of infrastructure limits.

Interim guidance caps flow in each conduit to minimize cavitation damage (the Draft SEIS modeled 3,150 cfs per tube, 12,600 cfs total); a 2023 inspection found the components sufficient for periodic releases but raised concern about long-term high-flow use, and Reclamation concluded it should not rely on the outlet works as the sole release path below 3,490 ft.

Significant alterations to the dam would require congressional authorization; Lower Basin states have criticized limiting infrastructure protection to reduced Lake Powell releases, calling it 'shortsighted' and a cause of 'major cuts' to Lower Basin deliveries, and objected that the post-2026 EIS did not address the dam's plumbing problems.

supporting_evidence.summary: Glen Canyon Dam's design-basis minimum water surface elevation for power operation is 3,490 feet, with the eight penstock intakes centered at elevation 3,470 feet (about 45 feet above the estimated silt elevation projected after 150 years of reservoir operation). Reflecting this design threshold, Reclamation's March 2024 interim operating guidance directs exercising the full extent of Upper Colorado Basin operational capabilities to attempt to maintain Lake Powell at or above elevation 3,490 ft, so as to preserve redundant downstream delivery through both the penstocks and the river outlet works.

Reclamation's original Technical Record of Design and Construction established elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum reservoir elevation for power production, 20 ft above the penstock intake centerline (elevation 3,470 ft); water cannot be released through the penstocks below 3,490 ft (OFF-025-03). Multiple later sources restate this same threshold: Reclamation estimates the depth for minimum power pool is 20 ft above the penstocks, i.e. elevation 3,490 fasl (CRS-002-02); at 3,490 ft, minimum power pool is 20 ft above the generators' actual penstock intakes, and the dam's eight turbines must be shut down at minimum power pool to avoid cavitation (MED-002-01); the 1999 multi-level intake structure hydraulic model study likewise designates elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum water surface for power operations (OFF-028-06); the 2016 LTEMP Final EIS states hydropower production would cease if Lake Powell drops below approximately 3,490 ft (OFF-005-01); the 2024 Near-term Operations SEIS ROD notes dry hydrology in recent years produced low Lake Powell elevations at levels such as 3,490 ft, giving Reclamation operating experience at this threshold (OFF-002-06); the 2024 LTEMP Final Supplemental EIS states Reclamation's Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels directs use of the full extent of Upper Colorado Basin operational capabilities to try to keep Lake Powell at or above elevation 3,490 ft (OFF-007-03); and an April 2026 status report reiterates that hydropower generation stops at 3,490 feet, with the reservoir at 3,526 feet at that time and Reclamation aiming to keep it above 3,500 feet (MED-001-04).

The river outlet works (four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes) were designed with an unrestricted capacity of 3,750 cfs per tube (15,000 cfs total) at reservoir elevation 3,490 ft (minimum power-operation water surface). Below elevation 3,550 ft, however, the 2024 LTEMP Final SEIS's modeling assumed a reduced capacity of 3,150 cfs per tube (12,600 cfs total) rather than the unrestricted 3,750 cfs/tube maximum. Separately, Reclamation's March 2024 interim operating guidance set even more granular, elevation-stepped interim maximum per-conduit flow limits to limit cavitation risk, including 3,185 cfs at elevation 3,490 ft, stepping down to 2,200 cfs at 3,420 ft, 1,200 cfs at 3,400 ft, and 0 cfs at 3,390 ft.

When Lake Powell drops below the minimum power pool elevation of 3,490 feet, Glen Canyon Dam can no longer release water through its powerplant turbines/penstocks and must rely on the river outlet works (ROW), whose capacity is limited and increases with pool elevation (OFF-021-08); the Post-2026 Draft EIS states the dam 'was not envisioned to operate below minimum power pool (elevation 3,490 feet)' and that below this elevation water must be released through the jet tubes at the end of the ROW instead of the penstocks (OFF-019-05). Across all anticipated post-2026 operating alternatives, releases from Lake Powell may fall below the alternative's specified release volume at elevations below 3,490 feet due to this infrastructure limitation (OFF-020-04). A separate study quantified the resulting shortfall: at elevation 3,430 feet, the ROW can discharge only 10,200 cfs (7.41 MAF/year), considerably less than the Law of the River's 8.23 MAF/year delivery requirement, and below the ROW's own elevation of 3,370 feet, approximately 1.89 MAF becomes inaccessible dead storage (CRS-002-08).

Multiple sources indicate the river outlet works (ROW) were not designed for, and cannot be fully relied upon for, long-term or high-flow releases at low Lake Powell levels. Reclamation's 2024 Technical Decision Memorandum found no design reference indicating the ROW were intended for long-term water conveyance at low reservoir levels; historically they were used only to augment powerplant/spillway discharges for short durations (e.g., about three months during 1983 flood releases, days to a week for high-flow experiments) (OFF-025-04). A 2023 special inspection found the hollow-jet valves, pipes, and ring-follower gates sufficient for periodic/seasonal releases but flagged concern about long-term high-flow use and recommended a major overhaul or replacement for high confidence in continuous long-term operation (OFF-025-05). This concern has historical precedent: on April 20, 1965, at reservoir elevation 3,490 ft with the ROW variably open, the dam's tailrace stabilization slab was undermined by a recirculating eddy from ROW operation and portions of it collapsed, because tailwater was 4-6 feet lower than had been predicted by physical modeling (OFF-025-06). More recently, in 2023, when the ROW were used for a high-flow release into the Grand Canyon at low-reservoir levels, damaging cavitation occurred, and the Bureau has warned further extended use would likely cause more (MED-002-03). Based on this evidence, Reclamation's formal conclusion is that it should not rely on the ROW as the sole means of releasing water from Glen Canyon Dam, as would be required below minimum power pool (3,490 ft), given current uncertainty about long-term conduit and hollow-jet valve performance and tailrace sedimentation (OFF-025-07).

The River Outlet Works (bypass tubes) have historically only been opened when the dam was first filled, during short-term high-flow experiments, and for emergency flood releases in the early 1980s, and have never been used over extended periods (EU-LP-CRS-002-03). Below minimum power pool, the River Outlet Works are the only remaining way to pass water through Glen Canyon Dam: two intakes leading to four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes with a combined maximum discharge capacity of 15,000 cubic feet per second (EU-LP-MED-002-02), a capacity figure confirmed on Reclamation's own project page, which also lists a combined spillway discharge capacity of 208,000 cfs at elevation 3,700.0 ft (EU-LP-OFF-030-02). Since the Draft SEIS, Reclamation identified enhanced risks associated with relying on the River Outlet Works as the exclusive means of releasing water at low reservoir elevations for sustained periods, prompting the 2024 Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels (EU-LP-OFF-007-04).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: Sources describe the 3,490 ft threshold differently: OFF-019 calls it the bottom of the penstock intake, while the design paper (OFF-027) gives the intake centerline at 3,470 ft and 3,490 ft as the minimum water surface for power. The per-conduit interim limits by elevation are in OFF-025 Table 1 and were not reproduced in the EUs. The stakeholder statements (CRS-001-12, MED-002-05) are positions, not findings.
items.operational_implication: Release planning at low storage cannot assume that the outlet works can deliver the scheduled annual volume; this physical ceiling is one reason the 3,490 ft elevation functions as an operating floor in the 2024 guidance.

items.title: The hourly and daily release envelope at Glen Canyon Dam: fixed limits, volume-dependent fluctuation, and defined exceptions
items.operational_question: Which limits define the allowable hourly and daily release pattern at Glen Canyon Dam under MLFF and LTEMP, and when can they be exceeded?
items.synthesis_claim: The sub-annual envelope combines fixed limits (minimum 8,000 cfs from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and 5,000 cfs at night; maximum 25,000 cfs for power generation), a daily fluctuation range that depends on the monthly release volume, and ramp-rate limits. LTEMP Alternative D replaced the MLFF three-step fluctuation table with a proportional rule (9 or 10 times the monthly volume in kaf) but kept 8,000 cfs as the maximum daily range in any month, and raised the down-ramp limit from 1,500 to 2,500 cfs/hr while keeping the 4,000 cfs/hr up-ramp. The maximum can be exceeded only in defined cases (very wet months, spill or flood avoidance, approved experiments such as HFEs, and emergencies), and WAPA's dispatch practices operate inside these limits without being ROD requirements.
items.scope_and_conditions: Base operations of Glen Canyon Dam under the 1996 ROD / 1997 Operating Criteria (MLFF) and the 2016 LTEMP ROD Alternative D, as carried into the 2024 LTEMP SEIS assumptions. Does not govern annual release volume, which is set under the LROC and the Interim Guidelines. Experimental flows (HFEs, trout management flows) and emergency exceptions are outside base operations.

analysis_chain.statement: Minimum releases are 8,000 cfs from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and 5,000 cfs at night, and maximum release for power generation is 25,000 cfs; the 1996 ROD raised the maximum from 20,000 to 25,000 cfs and the up-ramp from 2,500 to 4,000 cfs/hr between draft and final EIS to enhance power production flexibility.

MLFF limited daily fluctuation to 5,000, 6,000, or 8,000 cfs for monthly volumes below 600 kaf, 600-800 kaf, and above 800 kaf; LTEMP sets the range at 10 times the monthly volume in kaf in June-August and 9 times in other months, with 8,000 cfs as the maximum in any month, retained from the 1996 ROD for safety, recreation, and sediment reasons.

Under LTEMP the up-ramp remains 4,000 cfs/hr and the down-ramp is limited to 2,500 cfs/hr, which is 1,000 cfs/hr more than the No-Action (MLFF) limit of 1,500 cfs/hr; the 2024 SEIS assumes the same 4,000/2,500 cfs/hr rates.

The 25,000 cfs maximum may be exceeded when the average monthly release exceeds 25,000 cfs (released at a constant rate), to avoid spills or flood releases, under approved experiments such as the HFE protocol, and under emergency exception criteria, which suspend normal operations until the emergency ends or WAPA has discharged its reliability-council responsibility.

Within these limits WAPA maximizes releases in peak-demand periods (generally Monday-Saturday, 7 a.m.-11 p.m.) and follows other dispatch practices, which fall within MLFF constraints but are not ROD requirements and may be altered by WAPA at any time.

supporting_evidence.summary: Since the 1996 Record of Decision selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) alternative (codified in the 1997 Operating Criteria), Glen Canyon Dam releases have been bound by a consistent set of limits, repeated across CRS reports, LTEMP EIS chapters, biological opinions/assessments, GAO review, and peer-reviewed research: minimum release of 8,000 cfs from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and 5,000 cfs at night; maximum release of 25,000 cfs (well below the approximately 31,500 cfs turbine/penstock capacity, i.e. about 76% of unrestricted capacity at elevation 3,700 ft); ascending (up) ramp rate up to 4,000 cfs/hour; descending (down) ramp rate up to 1,500 cfs/hour; and an allowable daily flow fluctuation that scales with that month's total release volume -- 5,000 cfs/day for monthly release volumes under 0.6 maf (600 kaf), 6,000 cfs/day for 0.6-0.8 maf (600-800 kaf), and 8,000 cfs/day for volumes over 0.8 maf (800 kaf). A peer-reviewed research paper (RES-018) restates the same limits in metric units (141 m3/s minimum, 708 m3/s maximum, and 142/170/227 m3/s daily fluctuation tiers), confirming unit-equivalence with the cfs figures used elsewhere.

The 8,000 cfs maximum daily fluctuation limit (the top tier of the MLFF sliding-scale fluctuation rule) was established in the 1996 Record of Decision to address safety, recreation, and sediment concerns, based on a 1995 study (Reclamation 1995) of river-guide/public flow preferences. Under the LTEMP Final EIS (2016), this same 8,000 cfs cap is retained and is present in both the No Action Alternative and the LTEMP preferred alternative (Alternative D).

Under LTEMP Alternative D (the 2016 ROD selected alternative), the allowable within-day fluctuation range is no longer a fixed 3-tier schedule but a formula proportional to that month's scheduled release volume: 10 x monthly volume (kaf) in June-August, and 9 x monthly volume (kaf) in other months, subject to an overall cap (stated elsewhere as 227 m3/s, approximately 8,000 cfs). Alternative D also raises the down-ramp (descending) rate limit to no more than 2,500 cfs/hour (1,000 cfs/hour greater than the prior No-Action/MLFF limit of 1,500 cfs/hour), while retaining the up-ramp (ascending) rate at 4,000 cfs/hour, unchanged from MLFF. A companion research paper restates these LTEMP ramp rates in metric units: 113 m3/s/hour increasing (~4,000 cfs/hr) and 71 m3/s/hour decreasing (~2,500 cfs/hr), explicitly framed as a change made to reduce sandbar erosion rates.

Beginning November 1, 1991, Reclamation implemented interim operating criteria for Glen Canyon Dam that cut the approved maximum peak release from 31,500 cfs to 20,000 cfs, restricted daily fluctuations to a range of 5,000-8,000 cfs, and capped ramp rates at 2,500 cfs/hour increasing and 1,500 cfs/hour decreasing, while still meeting the 8.23 maf minimum annual release. Between the draft and final EIS that led to the 1996 Record of Decision, these same starting values were revised: the up-ramp rate limit was increased from 2,500 to 4,000 cfs/hour, and the maximum allowable release was increased from 20,000 to 25,000 cfs, specifically to enhance power production flexibility in response to public comments.

Under the 2016 LTEMP FEIS, when very wet hydrologic conditions occur (average monthly release rate above 25,000 cfs), Glen Canyon Dam may exceed the 25,000 cfs cap but must release at a constant rate; the limit may also be exceeded to avoid spills, during flood releases, for approved experimental high-flow-experiment (HFE) releases, or to accommodate electrical emergencies (EU-LP-OFF-005-06). Consistent with this, the 2007 Biological Assessment states the 25,000 cfs maximum flow limit under the 1996 ROD and 1997 Operating Criteria may be exceeded for emergency conditions and during extreme hydrological conditions, and notes that separate emergency exception criteria also apply during normal operations (EU-LP-OFF-011-16).

The Emergency Exception Criteria were established under Section 3 of the Glen Canyon Dam Operating Criteria (62 FR 9448, March 3, 1997) and continue unchanged under LTEMP Alternative D; when invoked, normal operations are suspended until the emergency has ended or WAPA has discharged its NERC responsibility regarding the emergency (EU-LP-OFF-003-09). The 1996 ROD establishes that these criteria allow WAPA to respond to various emergency situations consistent with its North American Electric Reliability Council (NERC) obligations, with exceptions to standard operating criteria during search-and-rescue situations, special studies and monitoring, dam and powerplant maintenance, and spinning reserves (EU-LP-OFF-008-06). GAO's 1997 assessment describes these deviations as usually lasting less than 4 hours, covering power and water emergencies such as insufficient generating capacity, restoration of the electrical system, or search-and-rescue operations (EU-LP-OFF-010-05). The underlying NERC standard requires a disturbance (sudden generation loss or transmission imbalance) be corrected within 10 minutes; Glen Canyon Dam's reserve capacity is also contractually used to restart tripped thermal powerplants and provide emergency shutdown power to nuclear powerplants, and responding to such electrical emergencies is exempt from 1996 ROD operating constraints (EU-LP-OFF-005-11).

Beyond formal ROD requirements, WAPA follows discretionary dispatch practices at Glen Canyon Dam -- such as holding nightly generation to the same minimum level during off-peak hours and keeping weekend releases at no less than 85 percent of the average weekday release -- that fall within MLFF constraints but are not ROD requirements and can be altered or abandoned by WAPA at any time (EU-LP-OFF-005-10). Per the 1997 GAO report, to the extent possible Glen Canyon Dam's hourly power operations followed three guidelines: maximize water releases during peak energy demand periods (generally Monday-Saturday, 7 a.m. to 11 p.m.); maximize releases during peak-demand months and minimize during low-demand months; and minimize or eliminate powerplant bypasses (EU-LP-OFF-010-13).

The LTEMP (including its 2016 ROD and 2024 SEIS amendment) governs only the monthly, daily, and hourly release pattern from Glen Canyon Dam. It does not control the total annual release volume, which remains governed separately by the Long-Range Operating Criteria (LROC) as currently implemented through the 2007 Interim Guidelines (and, for the 2024 amendment, as further supplemented by the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS). Because of this scope boundary, LTEMP does not modify determinations made under the Interim Shortage Guidelines for Lake Powell and Lake Mead and does not trigger an off-cycle mid-year review of reservoir operations.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: RES-018 describes LTEMP ramping rates as 'constrained ... to reduce sandbar erosion rates', but the LTEMP ROD shows the down-ramp limit was relaxed from 1,500 to 2,500 cfs/hr relative to MLFF; the sediment rationale in the ROD attaches to the more even monthly volume distribution and the retained 8,000 cfs cap. This card follows the ROD. The hourly dispatch guidelines in OFF-010 date from 1996.
items.operational_implication: Daily fluctuation in a given month can be computed from the scheduled monthly volume (9x or 10x kaf, capped at 8,000 cfs), so the allowed hydropower load-following range shrinks in low-volume years.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-003 resolved whether the proportional formula can exceed 8,000 cfs: 'The maximum allowable daily fluctuation range in flows in any month will be 8,000 cfs, which is also the maximum daily fluctuation range under Alternative A'; RES-018 likewise states the fluctuation is 'still capped at 227 m3/s'. OFF-003 also states the down-ramp 'will be limited to no greater than 2,500 cfs/hr, which is 1,000 cfs/hr greater than what is allowed under Alternative A', so the candidate claim that LTEMP tightened the down-ramp to reduce sandbar erosion was rejected. OFF-008 confirmed the 1996 up-ramp and maximum-release increases were made 'to enhance power production flexibility'.

items.title: Lake Powell's operating elevations form a stacked set of tiers, targets, and physical floors
items.operational_question: Which Lake Powell elevations trigger changes in release rules or operating response, and how do they relate to one another?
items.synthesis_claim: Different instruments attach operational meaning to a descending set of Lake Powell elevations: full pool at 3,700 ft; 3,630 ft as the 2004 interim 602(a) storage guideline for equalization; 3,575 ft and 3,525 ft as the 2007 Interim Guidelines tier boundaries; 3,525 ft also as the DROA target elevation, chosen as a 35 ft buffer for response actions; 3,500 ft as the 2024 Section 6.E elevation that the Secretary seeks to maintain by reducing releases to not less than 6.0 maf; 3,490 ft as minimum power pool, which the March 2024 guidance tries to hold; and about 3,370 ft as the river outlet works intake and dead pool. The upper levels select release volumes, the middle levels trigger protective actions, and the lowest levels are physical limits.
items.scope_and_conditions: Thresholds in force through 2026 under the 2007 Interim Guidelines, the 2019 DCP/DROA, the 2024 SEIS ROD, and Reclamation's March 2024 Interim Operating Guidance. Tier releases also depend on projected Lake Mead elevation (for example, 1,075 ft in the Upper Elevation Balancing Tier). Elevations use the datum of each source; the 2018 USGS survey reports NAVD88 values that differ slightly. Post-2026 guidelines may change these thresholds.

analysis_chain.statement: Equalization releases require Lake Powell above the Equalization Elevation Table level, with the 2004 interim 602(a) guideline at 3,630 ft; between that level and 3,575 ft the Secretary releases 8.23 maf if Lake Mead is projected at or above 1,075 ft; from 3,575 ft down to 3,525 ft the Mid-Elevation Release Tier applies; below 3,525 ft the Lower Elevation Balancing Tier balances contents with 7.0-9.5 maf releases.

DROA defines 3,525 ft as the target elevation for minimizing the risk of declining below 3,490 ft, a 35 ft buffer to allow response actions; operational adjustments in Glen Canyon Dam monthly volumes are considered first, and the parties state this elevation balances infrastructure protection, compact obligations, and Upper Division beneficial use.

Under Section 6.E, if the minimum probable 24-Month Study projects Lake Powell below 3,500 ft within 12 months, the Secretary begins planning to reduce releases to not less than 6.0 maf to maintain 3,500 ft; the 2024 SEIS also assumes no HFE below 3,500 ft.

Minimum power pool is 3,490 ft, which Reclamation's March 2024 guidance seeks to maintain so that penstocks and outlet works remain redundant release paths; the river outlet works intake at about 3,370 ft is described as dead pool, below which no other outlet exists.

supporting_evidence.summary: Reclamation's Upper Colorado Region CRSP Glen Canyon Unit Quick Facts page states Lake Powell's live capacity at elevation 3,700 feet is 24,322,000 acre-feet (OFF-029-01). The 2016 LTEMP Final EIS Chapter 3 similarly states Lake Powell has a maximum live storage capacity of about 24.3 maf (OFF-005-01), matching the Quick Facts figure.

Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines Section 6.A (Equalization Tier), if Lake Powell reaches the elevation stated in the Lake Powell Equalization Elevation Table for a given Water Year and the September 30 projected Lake Mead elevation is below 1,105 feet, the Secretary releases additional water from Lake Powell to Lake Mead until the reservoirs fully equalize, Lake Mead reaches 1,105 feet, or Lake Powell reaches 20 feet below its equalization elevation. Reclamation's 2004 interim 602(a) storage guideline, in effect through 2026, supplies the concrete current value implementing this mechanism: Lake Powell's elevation must be above 3,630 feet (approximately 14.85 maf of storage) for equalization releases between Lake Powell and Lake Mead to occur at all.

The Interim Guidelines for Coordinated Operations of Lake Powell and Lake Mead define four operating tiers -- the Equalization Tier, Upper Elevation Balancing Tier, Mid-Elevation Release Tier, and Lower Elevation Balancing Tier -- with scheduled Lake Powell water-year releases adjusted each month based on forecast inflow and projected September 30 elevations at both reservoirs. In CRSS modeling of the Continued Current Strategies baseline, each January's governing tier is set by end-of-calendar-year pool elevation: the Equalization Tier applies at or above the Equalization Level; the Upper Elevation Balancing Tier applies down to elevation 3,575 feet; the Mid-Elevation Release Tier applies between 3,575 and 3,525 feet; and the Lower Elevation Balancing Tier applies below elevation 3,525 feet.

Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines' Mid-Elevation Release Tier (Section 6.C), when the projected January 1 Lake Powell elevation is below 3,575 feet and at or above 3,525 feet, the Secretary releases 7.48 maf from Lake Powell in the Water Year if the projected January 1 Lake Mead elevation is at or above 1,025 feet (or 8.23 maf if Lake Mead is below 1,025 feet). Both the Draft 2026 Annual Operating Plan and the July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study confirm this Mid-Elevation Release Tier (per 2007 Interim Guidelines Section 6.C.1 and the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD Section 6.E) governs Lake Powell operations for Water Year 2026, with the August 2025 24-Month Study's most probable inflow scenario originally projecting a 7.48 maf release from Glen Canyon Dam for WY2026.

Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines' Lower Elevation Balancing Tier (Section 6.D), when the projected January 1 Lake Powell elevation is below 3,525 feet, the Secretary balances the contents of Lake Mead and Lake Powell but releases not more than 9.5 maf and not less than 7.0 maf from Lake Powell in the Water Year. The Post-2026 Colorado River Reservoir Operations Draft EIS describes its Basic Coordination Alternative (the least-restrictive of four proposed post-2026 alternatives) as providing Glen Canyon Dam releases of 7.0 to 9.5 maf depending on Lake Powell elevation, with the lowest releases occurring at or below a Lake Powell elevation of 3,525 feet -- the same numeric range and elevation threshold as the current Lower Elevation Balancing Tier.

The Drought Response Operations Agreement (DROA) defines elevation 3,525 ft as the 'target elevation' at Lake Powell for minimizing the risk of the reservoir declining below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool), providing a 35-foot buffer above minimum power pool to allow response actions before Lake Powell drops below 3,490 ft. Under DROA, operational adjustments in monthly release volumes at Glen Canyon Dam are considered first to minimize the risk of Lake Powell declining below this Target Elevation, before releases from other CRSPA Initial Units (e.g., Flaming Gorge, Navajo, Aspinall) are evaluated as a subsequent response option.

Under the Upper Basin DCP's DROA, Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above elevation 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool (EU-LP-CRS-001-04). Reclamation's stated operational goal under DROA is to 'protect' this 3,525-ft elevation, primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial-unit reservoirs (EU-LP-CRS-002-04). The DROA establishes the process for Reclamation, in collaboration with the Upper Basin States, to release additional water from upstream CRSP initial-unit reservoirs (Flaming Gorge, Aspinall, Navajo, Glen Canyon/Lake Powell) to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation (EU-LP-OFF-017-03). In CRSS modeling, Powell Infrastructure Protection (PIP) releases from the Upper Initial Units (Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Navajo) are specifically triggered when Lake Powell is projected to fall below elevation 3,525 feet (EU-LP-OFF-021-06). This target was actually invoked when the July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell declining below the 3,525.00-ft DROA target elevation, triggering DROA year-2025 drought-response planning under the DCP-related agreements (EU-LP-OFF-022-03); consistent with protecting this same target, the December 2025 24-Month Study reduced Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes for December 2025 through April 2026 by 0.598 maf (EU-LP-OFF-023-03).

Under the 2024 near-term consensus agreement / 2024 ROD's new Section XI.G.6.E (per CRS summary and the official Record of Decision), if the minimum probable 24-Month Study projects an elevation below 3,500 feet at Lake Powell in the next 12 months, the Secretary must begin planning to reduce Lake Powell releases as needed to not less than 6.0 maf for the Water Year to maintain elevation 3,500 feet -- in lieu of a 7.0 maf figure referenced under the near-term proposal framing.

Glen Canyon Dam's design-basis minimum water surface elevation for power operation is 3,490 feet, with the eight penstock intakes centered at elevation 3,470 feet (about 45 feet above the estimated silt elevation projected after 150 years of reservoir operation). Reflecting this design threshold, Reclamation's March 2024 interim operating guidance directs exercising the full extent of Upper Colorado Basin operational capabilities to attempt to maintain Lake Powell at or above elevation 3,490 ft, so as to preserve redundant downstream delivery through both the penstocks and the river outlet works.

Reclamation's original Technical Record of Design and Construction established elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum reservoir elevation for power production, 20 ft above the penstock intake centerline (elevation 3,470 ft); water cannot be released through the penstocks below 3,490 ft (OFF-025-03). Multiple later sources restate this same threshold: Reclamation estimates the depth for minimum power pool is 20 ft above the penstocks, i.e. elevation 3,490 fasl (CRS-002-02); at 3,490 ft, minimum power pool is 20 ft above the generators' actual penstock intakes, and the dam's eight turbines must be shut down at minimum power pool to avoid cavitation (MED-002-01); the 1999 multi-level intake structure hydraulic model study likewise designates elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum water surface for power operations (OFF-028-06); the 2016 LTEMP Final EIS states hydropower production would cease if Lake Powell drops below approximately 3,490 ft (OFF-005-01); the 2024 Near-term Operations SEIS ROD notes dry hydrology in recent years produced low Lake Powell elevations at levels such as 3,490 ft, giving Reclamation operating experience at this threshold (OFF-002-06); the 2024 LTEMP Final Supplemental EIS states Reclamation's Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels directs use of the full extent of Upper Colorado Basin operational capabilities to try to keep Lake Powell at or above elevation 3,490 ft (OFF-007-03); and an April 2026 status report reiterates that hydropower generation stops at 3,490 feet, with the reservoir at 3,526 feet at that time and Reclamation aiming to keep it above 3,500 feet (MED-001-04).

The 2016 LTEMP Final EIS states Glen Canyon Dam is designed to operate between the outlet works intake elevation of 3,370 ft AMSL and the top of the live storage pool at 3,700 ft AMSL (OFF-005-01). High Country News reporting states that if Lake Powell drops to the river outlet works' (ROW) elevation of 3,370 feet, the reservoir reaches "dead pool," where water passes through the dam only when river flow exceeds evaporation losses, with no lower intakes or spillways available (MED-002-04). The 2018 USGS resurvey, using the NAVD88 vertical datum, places the dead storage elevation (below all hydroelectric penstocks and other outlet works) at 3,372.91 ft NAVD88 (RES-013-04).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The 3,525 ft value serves two separate roles (tier boundary and DROA target) under different instruments; the evidence does not state that one was derived from the other. The dead-pool description at 3,370 ft is from a media source and a DEIS chapter; the 2018 USGS survey gives the dead storage elevation as 3,372.91 ft NAVD88. Whether the Equalization Elevation Table value for a given year equals 3,630 ft was not checked here.
items.operational_implication: When Lake Powell is reported at a given elevation, this stack shows which instrument governs the response at that level: a tier volume, a DROA action, a Section 6.E reduction, or a physical limit.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-031 confirmed the buffer rationale: 'The target elevation provides a 35-foot buffer above minimum power pool (elevation 3,490 feet) to allow for response actions'. OFF-001 confirmed tier boundaries are based on 'the projected January 1 Lake Powell elevation' and that the Upper Elevation Balancing Tier 8.23 maf release is conditioned on Lake Mead at or above 1,075 ft. The candidate claim was qualified to note that the tier boundary and the DROA target share a value but come from different instruments.

items.title: Restrictions on hourly release patterns trade hydropower value against downstream resources
items.operational_question: How have Glen Canyon Dam's sub-annual release restrictions traded hydropower value against downstream resource objectives, and how large has the hydropower cost been?
items.synthesis_claim: Both major sub-annual operating decisions were made as explicit tradeoffs. The 1996 ROD selected MLFF knowing it would cause 'a significant loss of hydropower benefits' (estimated at $15.1-44.2 million per year, 1991 dollars) and justified it with a non-use value study; an ex post reanalysis put the realized average at $26.3 million per year in 1991 dollars ($39 million in 2009 dollars), and the LTEMP FEIS reports an average annual cost of $38-50 million for 1997-2005. For LTEMP, no alternative dominated across metrics and the preferred alternative depended on stakeholder weights; Alternative D was selected with an expected 1.1% decrease in average daily generation and 6.7% decrease in firm capacity relative to No Action. Bypass releases add a further cost because water passed around the generators produces no energy.
items.scope_and_conditions: Hydropower economics of Glen Canyon Dam under the 1996 ROD (MLFF) and the 2016 LTEMP ROD. Dollar values are reported in different bases: the ex ante and ex post figures in RES-026 are stated in 1991 dollars (and 2009 dollars), while OFF-005 does not state a dollar year for its $38-50 million range. Percentages for Alternative D are relative to the No-Action Alternative.

analysis_chain.statement: MLFF restrictions reduced the operating flexibility of the hydropower plant and therefore its economic value, and prompted WAPA to modify commitments to its customers.

The 1996 ROD estimated a loss of $15.1-44.2 million per year (1991 dollars); the ex post analysis estimated an average of $26.3 million (1991 dollars) or $39 million (2009 dollars), and the LTEMP FEIS reports an average annual cost of $38-50 million for 1997-2005 due to operational restrictions; GAO noted the original hydropower analysis did not include price elasticity.

analysis_chain.stage: stated basis for accepting the cost
analysis_chain.statement: The 1996 ROD cited a non-use value study indicating willingness to pay more than this loss to maintain a healthy Grand Canyon ecosystem; the EIS team had concluded that none of the alternatives could maximize benefits to all resources.

In the LTEMP decision analysis no strategy dominated across metrics; Alternative B ranked highest for stakeholders valuing hydropower and others for those weighting other resources. Alternative D was selected with an expected 1.1% decrease in average daily generation and 6.7% decrease in firm capacity relative to No Action.

Experimental and high releases beyond powerplant capacity bypass the generators, producing no energy, possibly requiring replacement power purchases, and raising tailwater stage, which reduces effective head.

supporting_evidence.summary: The 1996 ROD's Modified Low Fluctuating Flow operating criteria reduced Glen Canyon Dam powerplant's operating flexibility and therefore its economic value, prompting the Western Area Power Administration to modify commitments it had made to its customers.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; abstract

supporting_evidence.summary: Reclamation estimated the selected MLFF alternative would cause a significant loss of hydropower benefits (between $15.1 million and $44.2 million annually) but determined this loss was outweighed by a non-use value study indicating the American public is willing to pay substantially more than this amount to maintain a healthy Grand Canyon ecosystem.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section VII Basis for Decision

supporting_evidence.summary: The ex ante (pre-ROD) analysis estimated the 1996 ROD's power economic impacts at $15.1 million to $44.2 million annually (1991 dollars); this ex post reanalysis using actual 1997-2005 market data found average impacts of $26.3 million (1991$), equivalent to $39 million in 2009 dollars.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; abstract

supporting_evidence.summary: MLFF ramping restrictions prevent Glen Canyon Dam generation from adjusting hourly to match power customer demand, forcing increased reliance on alternate generating resources; between 1997 and 2005 this operational restriction cost WAPA and its power customers an average of $38 million to $50 million per year.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section 3.13.1.4 Scheduling

supporting_evidence.summary: GAO found that the Power Resources Committee's hydropower cost-impact analysis omitted price elasticity (the demand-reducing effect of higher electricity prices), assumed an 8-percent annual natural gas price escalation through 2010 versus contemporary industry forecasts of 5-6 percent, and contained two uncorrected computational errors, all of which reduce the precision of the estimated economic impacts of the flow alternatives.
