supporting_evidence.summary: The EIS team concluded that none of the nine flow alternatives could simultaneously maximize benefits across all 11 studied resources (including hydropower), so selecting a preferred alternative required explicit trade-offs between downstream resource protection (fish, sediment, cultural resources, recreation) and hydropower flexibility.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Chapter 3, Reclamation's Process for Selecting a Preferred Alternative (~p. 49-50)

supporting_evidence.summary: The 19 LTEMP long-term strategies produced unavoidable tradeoffs across performance metrics, with no strategy dominating all others; depending on which stakeholder weights were applied, three alternatives (B, D, and G) were top-ranked, with Alternative B favored by hydropower-focused stakeholders, G by those valuing natural-process restoration, and D by the remaining stakeholders.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Abstract

supporting_evidence.summary: Selecting Alternative D reflects an explicit, quantified tradeoff between hydropower production and downstream ecological/sediment resources: relative to the No-Action Alternative it is expected to decrease average daily hydropower generation by 1.1 percent and firm capacity by 6.7 percent, while improving sandbar-building potential by 152 percent and humpback chub and vegetation conditions.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section 4.3 Performance of Alternative D

supporting_evidence.summary: Bypassing water around the Glen Canyon powerplant generators (e.g., during HFEs or high releases beyond turbine capacity) produces no hydroelectric energy, forces WAPA to purchase replacement power, and raises tailwater stage, which reduces effective head and power-conversion efficiency at the turbines.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section 3.13.1.3 Operational Flexibility

supporting_evidence.summary: The 1996 ROD's Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) operating criteria reduced Glen Canyon Dam powerplant's operating flexibility and, consequently, its economic value. An ex post economic analysis found this reduction in flexibility prompted the Western Area Power Administration (WAPA) to modify commitments made to its customers (RES-026-01). A separate LTEMP EIS accounting found that between 1997 and 2005, this operational restriction cost WAPA and its power customers an average of $38 million to $50 million per year, since MLFF ramping restrictions prevented generation from adjusting hourly to match power demand, forcing increased reliance on alternate generating resources (OFF-005-08).

In the 1996 Record of Decision, the Secretary selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) Alternative as Glen Canyon Dam's operating criteria, explicitly because it would reduce daily flow fluctuations well below the 'no action' (historic peaking) levels of releases while providing high steady releases of short duration to protect or enhance downstream resources, allowing limited flexibility for power operations. A peer-reviewed research paper confirms MLFF became the dam's operating regime in 1996, replacing hydroelectric peaking operations, and was the preferred alternative identified in the 1995 Environmental Impact Statement as an adaptive strategy for improving downstream Colorado River ecosystem resources.

Evaluation of Glen Canyon Dam LTEMP operating alternatives used a formal swing-weighting multicriteria decision-analysis (MCDA) process, developed with the USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center using the Simple Multi-Attribute Rating Technique (SMART): participating stakeholders ranked and weighted the importance of each performance metric according to its range of effect on resources. This MCDA approach, together with expected-value-of-information (EVPI/EVXI) analysis, was formally used to evaluate 19 long-term strategies against 18 performance metrics and to assess how much uncertainty mattered to the ranking of alternatives. The LTEMP EIS notes this decision-analysis process informed, but was not the sole basis for, selecting the preferred alternative.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: OFF-005 cites Veselka et al. (2010) for the $38-50 million range without a dollar year, while RES-026 reports $26.3 million (1991 dollars) / $39 million (2009 dollars); the evidence does not establish whether these are the same estimate in different dollar bases. The downstream benefits are described qualitatively or through a non-use value study and are not quantified in the same units as the hydropower cost.
items.operational_implication: Questions about the cost of environmental flow restrictions need the dollar basis and the period of each estimate; the record supports a cost in the tens of millions of dollars per year under MLFF, not a single figure.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-008 confirmed: 'Although there would be a significant loss of hydropower benefits due to the selection of the preferred alternative (between $15.1 and $44.2 million annually) a recently completed non-use value study ... indicates that the American people are willing to pay much more than this loss'. RES-026 confirmed the ex post average 'on average $26.3 million in $1991, or $39 million in $2009'. OFF-005 confirmed the '$38 million to $50 million' figure is attributed to Veselka et al. 2010 with no dollar year stated. The candidate claim, which equated the two estimates, was narrowed to report them separately.

items.title: Protecting Lake Powell's elevation shifts drought risk to Lake Mead and Lower Basin deliveries
items.operational_question: What does reducing Lake Powell releases to protect Glen Canyon Dam infrastructure trade off against downstream?
items.synthesis_claim: Holding water in Lake Powell and keeping it in Lake Mead are linked through the same release decision. The 2026 reduction from 7.48 to 6.0 maf was adopted because, absent intervention, Lake Powell was projected to fall below minimum power pool; Reclamation acknowledged that the reduction will accelerate Lake Mead's decline, with potential for up to an additional 40% reduction in Hoover Dam generating capacity. A 6.0 maf release is also below the roughly 8.25 maf average annual flow that the Upper Basin is understood to pass under the Compact and the 1944 treaty, and the Compact's obligation is measured as a 75 maf aggregate over ten consecutive years at Lee Ferry. The DROA describes its 3,525 ft target as balancing infrastructure protection and compact obligations with Upper Division beneficial use, and the post-2026 DEIS frames the same tension as its 'central tradeoff'.
items.scope_and_conditions: Water Year 2026 operations and the post-2026 planning context. The 8.25 maf figure is CRS's interpretation of the Compact plus half of the 1944 treaty obligation, not a release rule. Whether the 2026 reduction causes a Compact shortfall depends on the ten-year aggregate, which is not in this evidence set; the statement that it 'will likely' do so is from a media source quoting a legal practitioner.

analysis_chain.statement: Reclamation stated that without 0.66-1.0 maf of Flaming Gorge releases and 1.48 maf of reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases, Lake Powell would fall below minimum power pool (3,490 ft) by August 2026.
The DROA target of 3,525 ft is described by the parties as balancing the need to protect infrastructure, compact obligations, and Glen Canyon Dam operations with Upper Division beneficial use.
Reclamation acknowledges the reduced releases will accelerate Lake Mead's decline, with potential for up to an additional 40% reduction to Hoover Dam's generating capacity as early as fall 2026.

Under Compact Article III(d) the Upper Division states will not cause Lee Ferry flow to be depleted below 75 maf in any ten consecutive years; with the 1944 treaty share, CRS describes an average of at least 8.25 maf per year passing to the Lower Basin; the 1948 Upper Basin Compact assigns curtailment to states that overdrew their apportionment. A media source reports that the 6.0 maf release will likely push the ten-year total below the required threshold.

The post-2026 DEIS states that critically low storage, hydrologic variability, and drier expected conditions amplify the central tradeoff between the impacts of delivery reductions and the need to maintain reservoir storage.

supporting_evidence.summary: Absent major interventions—660,000 AF to 1 MAF of additional releases from Flaming Gorge Reservoir and 1.48 MAF of reduced Lower Basin releases from Glen Canyon Dam—Reclamation projected Lake Powell would fall below minimum power pool (3,490 feet) by August 2026.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Recent Conditions

supporting_evidence.summary: The Parties agree that the 3,525-foot Target Elevation appropriately balances the need to protect infrastructure, Colorado River Compact obligations, and Glen Canyon Dam operations as storage approaches minimum power pool against the Upper Division States' rights to put Colorado River System water to beneficial use.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Attachment A1, Section II.A.2

supporting_evidence.summary: Reclamation acknowledges that reducing Lake Powell releases to protect its elevation will accelerate the downstream decline of Lake Mead, with potential for up to an additional 40 percent reduction to Hoover Dam's hydropower generating capacity as early as fall 2026, directly trading Lake Powell protection against Lake Mead storage and Hoover Dam power generation.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; news release body, Basin-wide impacts

supporting_evidence.summary: Article III(d) requires that the States of the Upper Division not cause the flow of the Colorado River at Lee Ferry to be depleted below an aggregate of 75,000,000 acre-feet for any 10 consecutive years.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Article III(d)

supporting_evidence.summary: Pursuant to the 1922 Colorado River Compact and the 1944 Mexican Water Treaty, the Upper Basin must bypass an average of at least 8.25 million acre-feet per year through Glen Canyon Dam to the Lower Basin.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Background on Federal Development of the Colorado River Basin section

supporting_evidence.summary: Under Article IV, when curtailment of Upper Division use becomes necessary to maintain required Lee Ferry flow, the Upper Colorado River Commission determines curtailment by state, first requiring any state that overdrew its Article III apportionment in the preceding ten years to supply water at Lee Ferry equal to its overdraft before curtailment is imposed on other states.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Article IV(b), near line 100

supporting_evidence.summary: Cutting Lake Powell outflows to 6 million acre-feet in 2026 will likely push the required 10-year aggregate Lee Ferry delivery total below the Colorado River Compact's 75-million-acre-foot threshold (roughly 82.5 million acre-feet including Mexico's share), raising the prospect of first-ever interstate lawsuits over Colorado River supply.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; article body

supporting_evidence.summary: Developing new post-2026 guidelines is difficult because critically low storage, significant hydrologic variability, and anticipated drier conditions amplify the central tradeoff between the impacts of water-delivery reductions and the need to maintain reservoir storage.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; 1.1 Introduction

supporting_evidence.summary: On April 17, 2026, the Bureau of Reclamation announced unprecedented actions to store more water in Lake Powell -- then less than 25 percent full -- to preserve hydropower generation and protect Glen Canyon Dam water-delivery infrastructure the agency said was at risk from low reservoir levels (EU-LP-MED-001-01). With the consent of the four Upper Basin states, Reclamation committed to releasing between 660,000 and 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (82 percent full) into Lake Powell over the 12 months following the announcement, building on a smaller 463,000-acre-foot release used to prop up Powell in 2022-23 (EU-LP-MED-001-02). Because WY2026 was historically dry and Lake Powell was projected to decline below elevation 3,500 feet, the Department of the Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to reduce Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, coupled with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing approximately 660,000 to 1.00 maf of additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to Lake Powell by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-023-02). Reclamation's newsroom release confirms the combined plan: adding about 2.48 million acre-feet via the 660,000 AF-1 maf Flaming Gorge release (April 2026-April 2027, under the 2019 Drought Response Operating Agreements) plus the 7.48-to-6.0-maf release reduction through September 2026 under Section 6E, together expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation about 54 feet to at least 3,500 feet by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-035-02).

The Drought Response Operations Agreement (DROA) defines elevation 3,525 ft as the 'target elevation' at Lake Powell for minimizing the risk of the reservoir declining below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool), providing a 35-foot buffer above minimum power pool to allow response actions before Lake Powell drops below 3,490 ft. Under DROA, operational adjustments in monthly release volumes at Glen Canyon Dam are considered first to minimize the risk of Lake Powell declining below this Target Elevation, before releases from other CRSPA Initial Units (e.g., Flaming Gorge, Navajo, Aspinall) are evaluated as a subsequent response option.

The Colorado River Compact of 1922 apportions the exclusive beneficial consumptive use of 7,500,000 acre-feet (7.5 MAF) of water per year, in perpetuity, to each of the Upper Basin and the Lower Basin (Compact Article III(a)). A CRS congressional report restates this same 7.5 MAF-per-basin apportionment and adds that the Lower Basin was also given the right to increase its beneficial consumptive use by an additional 1 MAF per year.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: No document in this evidence set reports the ten-year Lee Ferry aggregate, so whether a Compact shortfall occurs cannot be determined here; the media statement is an expert opinion. The 40% Hoover figure is stated as a potential maximum. Lower Basin conservation actions intended to offset the Lake Mead decline are mentioned in OFF-035 but not quantified in the EUs.
items.operational_implication: A Lake Powell release cut should not be described as a net gain in storage for the system; it is a reallocation of risk between the two reservoirs and between basins, with possible legal consequences under the Compact.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-035 confirmed the wording 'Reclamation acknowledges that the proposed reduced releases from Lake Powell will accelerate the downstream decline of Lake Mead, with the potential for up to an additional 40% reduction to Hoover Dam's hydropower generating capacity'. MED-001 context shows the Compact-shortfall statement is the article's assessment introduced alongside a quoted attorney, not an agency finding. CRS-002 confirmed the 8.25 maf is derived from the Compact plus the 1944 treaty share 'generally understood to be shared equally'. Confidence was set to medium and the Compact-shortfall link was kept as an attributed opinion.

items.title: Low storage warms releases, and cooling them costs hydropower
items.operational_question: How does Lake Powell's storage level create a tradeoff between native fish, nonnative fish, and hydropower through release temperature?
items.synthesis_claim: Because the penstock intakes are fixed at about 3,470 ft, falling reservoir levels draw warmer water and raise release temperatures. Warming has been cited as a possible factor in humpback chub increases, but agencies and ecosystem modeling identify a parallel risk of warmwater nonnative fish predation. After smallmouth bass were detected spawning below the dam, the 2024 LTEMP SEIS adopted the Cool Mix Alternative, which bypasses colder water around the turbines when river-mile-61 temperatures exceed 15.5 °C for three consecutive days; in 2024 it ran from July 9 to November 18 and bypassed about 0.894 maf. The SEIS found bypass alternatives have the largest hydropower and replacement-power impacts, with four-year financial effects across alternatives ranging from a $0.14 million gain to a $222.03 million cost.
items.scope_and_conditions: Glen Canyon Dam release temperatures from the 2003-2011 drawdown through 2024 Cool Mix implementation. The 15.5 °C at river mile 61 trigger is stated for 2024; the 2026 AOP describes the trigger location differently (see KC-LP-EMR-15), so trigger details may vary by year. Financial figures cover the 2024-2027 SEIS operating period across all action alternatives, not Cool Mix alone.

analysis_chain.statement: With penstocks at a fixed elevation, high reservoir levels draw cooler hypolimnetic water, while low levels draw from the metalimnion or upper hypolimnion and releases are warmer.

River warming in 2003-2011 and 2014, caused by reduced storage, was expected to benefit native fish, but the Grand Canyon Ecosystem Model predicts nonnative fish will also benefit, potentially increasing risk to humpback chub; the 2008 Biological Opinion records Reclamation's commitment to monitor and control nonnative fish if warming occurs.

The 2024 SEIS was prompted by detection of smallmouth bass and other warmwater nonnative species directly below the dam; the Cool Mix trigger for 2024 was river-mile-61 temperatures above 15.5 °C for three consecutive days, and Cool Mix ran July 9-November 18, 2024, bypassing about 0.894 maf.

Water bypassed around the generators produces no energy; the SEIS found impacts on generation, replacement power, the Basin Fund, and transmission would be greatest under the Cool Mix alternatives, that WAPA may be unable to buy hundreds of MW per hour for months, and that four-year financial impacts range from a net gain of $140,000 to a cost of $222.03 million.

A 1999 Reclamation study of a multi-level intake structure aimed to release water at a temperature benefiting both native and nonnative fisheries while keeping warmwater nonnative species from moving upstream from Lake Mead.

supporting_evidence.summary: Because Glen Canyon Dam's penstock intakes sit at a fixed elevation of 3,470 ft, release water temperature depends on current reservoir level: when Lake Powell is high, releases are drawn from the cooler hypolimnion, but when reservoir levels are low, withdrawals shift to the warmer metalimnion or upper hypolimnion.

supporting_evidence.summary: Estimated financial impacts of the proposed action alternatives over the 4-year (2024-2027) operating period range from a net gain of $140,000 to a net cost of $222.03 million, depending on the alternative and the volume of replacement power that must be purchased; WAPA had already modified firm power rates for fiscal year 2022 partly because drought-driven low Lake Powell releases reduced power production.

supporting_evidence.summary: Since dam construction, water released below Glen Canyon Dam through the low-level penstock intakes has been a near-constant 45 degrees F (versus a pre-dam range from near-freezing to about 85 degrees F), which is tolerated by the nonnative trout fishery but is a threat to native fish (humpback chub and Colorado pikeminnow); the MLIS aims to release water benefiting both fisheries while keeping unwanted nonnative warm-water species from moving upstream from Lake Mead.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Project Background

supporting_evidence.summary: Reduced Lake Powell storage, by warming Glen Canyon Dam releases, has been identified as a risk pathway for increased nonnative-fish predation and competition pressure on humpback chub. River warming that occurred from 2003 to 2011 (and again in 2014), resulting from reduced Lake Powell storage, was intended to benefit native humpback chub, but the Grand Canyon Ecosystem Model predicted that nonnative fish would also benefit, potentially increasing predation/competition risk to humpback chub through greater fish interactions in critical river segments (RES-014-06). Consistent with this risk pathway, the 2008 Final Biological Opinion notes that because prolonged droughts (paleoclimate tree-ring records show droughts of 15-20 years) could lower Lake Powell storage and raise dam release temperatures, increasing nonnative predation risk to humpback chub, Reclamation committed to monitor and control nonnative fish as necessary through the Adaptive Management Program if such warming occurs (OFF-012-18).

Per the 2024 SEIS, for 2024 implementation the Cool Mix Alternative is triggered when average observed daily water temperature at river mile 61 (Little Colorado River confluence) exceeds 15.5°C (60°F) for three consecutive days, continuing until release temperatures fall back below that threshold at the target location (EU-LP-OFF-007-15). The 2026 Draft Annual Operating Plan describes the Cool Mix Alternative as triggered once average daily water temperature at river mile 30 reaches 15.5°C for three consecutive days, and states it was implemented from July 9 to November 18, 2024 (bypassing approximately 0.894 maf of water) and was reinitiated in August 2025 (EU-LP-OFF-022-09).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The evidence does not report whether the 2024 Cool Mix operation reduced smallmouth bass spawning, so its ecological effectiveness is not established here. The financial range spans all SEIS action alternatives; the Cool Mix-specific 2024 cost is in OFF-007 but not captured in an EU. The humpback chub benefit from warming is described in the sources as a possible factor, not an established cause.
items.operational_implication: Low storage affects downstream ecology through temperature as well as through water supply, and the main operating tool for cooling releases reduces hydropower at the same time that low head is already reducing it.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-012 confirmed the dual framing: 'increased release temperatures have been cited as one potential factor in the recent increase of young-of-year and juvenile humpback chub ... but concerns also exist that warmer aquatic habitat will also increase the risk of warm-water nonnative fish predation'. OFF-007 confirmed the 2024 trigger ('river mile 61, exceed 15.5°C (60°F) for three consecutive days') and that impacts 'would be greatest under the Cool Mix Alternative and the Cool Mix with Flow Spike Alternative'. OFF-022 confirmed the 2024 implementation dates and the 0.894 maf bypass. The humpback chub benefit was kept as a possible factor rather than a cause.

items.title: From hydropower peaking to conservative interim limits, then partial relaxation under MLFF and LTEMP
items.operational_question: How did Glen Canyon Dam's hourly and daily operating regime change from 1964 to the 2016 LTEMP, and which limits were tightened or relaxed at each step?
items.synthesis_claim: Sub-annual operations moved through three regimes. From 1964 to 1991 the dam was operated for peaking power, with releases up to turbine capacity (31,500 cfs) and river stage below the dam changing by as much as 14 feet a day. Interim criteria in 1991 imposed deliberately conservative limits: a 20,000 cfs maximum, 5,000-8,000 cfs daily fluctuation, and ramp rates of 2,500 cfs/hr up and 1,500 cfs/hr down. The 1996 ROD adopted these criteria with modifications as MLFF, raising the maximum to 25,000 cfs and the up-ramp to 4,000 cfs/hr for power flexibility, and the 2016 LTEMP ROD later raised the down-ramp to 2,500 cfs/hr while keeping the 8,000 cfs daily fluctuation cap. Each later step therefore relaxed some interim limits for hydropower while retaining the core fluctuation constraint.
items.scope_and_conditions: Sub-annual (hourly/daily) operating criteria at Glen Canyon Dam only; annual volumes were governed separately by the LROC throughout. Final 1996-ROD operating criteria were signed in February 1997. Sources differ on the date of the interim criteria (established August 1991 per RES-019; implemented November 1, 1991 per OFF-010 and OFF-009).

analysis_chain.statement: From 1964 to 1991 releases were adjusted daily and at times hourly to meet electrical demand, with river levels below the dam rising and falling by as much as 14 feet a day; before June 1990 daily maxima reached turbine capacity of 31,500 cfs.

To protect downstream resources until the EIS was complete, interim criteria reduced peak releases from 31,500 to 20,000 cfs, restricted daily fluctuation to 5,000-8,000 cfs, and limited ramp rates to 2,500 cfs/hr increasing and 1,500 cfs/hr decreasing; flows generally ranged 5,000-20,000 cfs until final criteria were signed in February 1997.

Under the Grand Canyon Protection Act process the Secretary issued the 1996 ROD selecting MLFF to reduce daily fluctuations well below historic levels while allowing limited power flexibility; between draft and final EIS the up-ramp was raised from 2,500 to 4,000 cfs/hr and the maximum release from 20,000 to 25,000 cfs to enhance power production flexibility.
The 2016 LTEMP ROD selected Alternative D, which set the down-ramp at 2,500 cfs/hr (1,000 cfs/hr more than under MLFF) and retained the 8,000 cfs maximum daily fluctuation established in 1996.

supporting_evidence.summary: Beginning November 1, 1991, Reclamation implemented interim operating criteria for Glen Canyon Dam that cut the approved maximum peak release from 31,500 cfs to 20,000 cfs, restricted daily fluctuations to a range of 5,000-8,000 cfs, and capped ramp rates at 2,500 cfs/hour increasing and 1,500 cfs/hour decreasing, while still meeting the 8.23 maf minimum annual release. Between the draft and final EIS that led to the 1996 Record of Decision, these same starting values were revised: the up-ramp rate limit was increased from 2,500 to 4,000 cfs/hour, and the maximum allowable release was increased from 20,000 to 25,000 cfs, specifically to enhance power production flexibility in response to public comments.

In the 1996 Record of Decision, the Secretary selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) Alternative as Glen Canyon Dam's operating criteria, explicitly because it would reduce daily flow fluctuations well below the 'no action' (historic peaking) levels of releases while providing high steady releases of short duration to protect or enhance downstream resources, allowing limited flexibility for power operations. A peer-reviewed research paper confirms MLFF became the dam's operating regime in 1996, replacing hydroelectric peaking operations, and was the preferred alternative identified in the 1995 Environmental Impact Statement as an adaptive strategy for improving downstream Colorado River ecosystem resources.

Two sources describe the origin of the interim operating criteria that were later adopted as the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) regime via the 1996 Record of Decision, but they give different establishment dates. Reclamation's 2002 Report to Congress states the Secretary adopted interim operating criteria in November 1991 limiting Glen Canyon Dam minimum/maximum flows and daily fluctuations, later superseded by final operating criteria signed February 1997 (62 Fed. Reg. 9447) that cap releases at 25,000 cfs except during high inflow years or power system emergencies. A USGS historical data report instead states the 1996 ROD adopted, with slight modification, interim operating criteria established in August 1991 as the MLFF alternative. This date discrepancy (August vs. November 1991) is preserved here rather than resolved, since the underlying source excerpts do not clarify whether they refer to the same milestone (e.g., proposal versus formal Secretarial adoption).

The 8,000 cfs maximum daily fluctuation limit (the top tier of the MLFF sliding-scale fluctuation rule) was established in the 1996 Record of Decision to address safety, recreation, and sediment concerns, based on a 1995 study (Reclamation 1995) of river-guide/public flow preferences. Under the LTEMP Final EIS (2016), this same 8,000 cfs cap is retained and is present in both the No Action Alternative and the LTEMP preferred alternative (Alternative D).

Under LTEMP Alternative D (the 2016 ROD selected alternative), the allowable within-day fluctuation range is no longer a fixed 3-tier schedule but a formula proportional to that month's scheduled release volume: 10 x monthly volume (kaf) in June-August, and 9 x monthly volume (kaf) in other months, subject to an overall cap (stated elsewhere as 227 m3/s, approximately 8,000 cfs). Alternative D also raises the down-ramp (descending) rate limit to no more than 2,500 cfs/hour (1,000 cfs/hour greater than the prior No-Action/MLFF limit of 1,500 cfs/hour), while retaining the up-ramp (ascending) rate at 4,000 cfs/hour, unchanged from MLFF. A companion research paper restates these LTEMP ramp rates in metric units: 113 m3/s/hour increasing (~4,000 cfs/hr) and 71 m3/s/hour decreasing (~2,500 cfs/hr), explicitly framed as a change made to reduce sandbar erosion rates.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The interim criteria date is reported as August 1991 (RES-019) and November 1, 1991 (OFF-010, OFF-009); the evidence does not resolve whether these are adoption and implementation dates. The 1991 down-ramp of 1,500 cfs/hr equals the MLFF value, so the 1996 ROD left that limit unchanged. The 2024 LTEMP SEIS (Cool Mix and flow options) is a further change in the temperature-management regime and is treated in a separate card.
items.operational_implication: Limits quoted for 'MLFF' or 'LTEMP' differ in maximum release and ramp rates; answers about allowable flows must name the regime and date.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-010 confirmed the interim criteria, implemented 'on November 1, 1991', restricted ramp rates 'to 2,500 cfs per hour when increasing and to 1,500 cfs per hour when decreasing' and were 'purposely designed to be conservative'. items.title: Annual-release rules have been layered on the 1970 LROC in response to drought, and most layers expire in 2026
items.operational_question: How has the framework governing Lake Powell's annual release volume changed since 1970, and what happens when the current interim instruments expire?
items.synthesis_claim: The annual-release regime has been built up in layers rather than replaced. The 1970 LROC set the objective of a minimum 8.23 maf annual release. After system storage fell from 55.8 maf (about 94% of capacity) in 1999 to 32.1 maf (about 54%) in 2007, the 2007 Interim Guidelines added elevation-based coordinated tiers to give water users predictability under drought. The 2019 DCPs added a Lake Mead Tier Zero shortage and the Upper Basin Drought Response Operations, which release water from upstream CRSP reservoirs to protect Lake Powell. The 2024 SEIS ROD adjusted the 2007 Guidelines, including the Section 6.E release reduction to as low as 6.0 maf. The 2007 Guidelines, the DCPs, and Minutes 323 and 330 are set to expire at the end of 2026; Interior began the post-2026 NEPA process in June 2023, and the No Action Alternative would revert to annual AOP determinations under pre-2007 guidance.
items.scope_and_conditions: Annual-volume framework for Glen Canyon Dam and its coordination with Lake Mead, 1970 to the January 2026 post-2026 DEIS. Sub-annual (hourly/daily) rules are covered separately. The post-2026 guidelines were not final in the evidence set, and the Secretary's intended ~20-year term is stated as open to a shorter duration.

analysis_chain.statement: The 1970 LROC set the objective of maintaining a minimum annual release from Lake Powell of 8.23 maf.
From October 1999 to September 2007, Colorado River reservoir storage fell from 55.8 maf (about 94% of capacity) to 32.1 maf (about 54%), reaching 29.7 maf in 2004.

The 2007 Interim Guidelines were developed to improve supply management and give water users more predictability about annual deliveries, particularly under drought and low reservoir conditions, and are implemented each year through the AOP.

The 2019 DCPs overlaid a Tier Zero shortage at Lake Mead elevations up to 1,090 ft and established Drought Response Operations to release water from upstream CRSP initial units to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation; the 2024 ROD adjusted the 2007 Guidelines, adding Section 6.E to reduce Lake Powell releases to not less than 6.0 maf to maintain 3,500 ft.

The 2007 Guidelines, 2019 DCPs, and Minutes 323 and 330 are set to expire at the end of 2026; Interior initiated the post-2026 NEPA process on June 16, 2023, intends a successor interim period of about 20 years, and the No Action Alternative assumes reversion to annual AOP determinations based on guidance in place before 2007.

supporting_evidence.summary: The 1970 Criteria for Coordinated Long-Range Operation of Colorado River Reservoirs (LROC), Article II(2), establishes the objective of maintaining a minimum annual release from Lake Powell of 8.23 million acre-feet (maf). Reclamation returned to this objective minimum release beginning in 1988 after the 1980-1987 Long-Range Operating Criteria period. The 2007 Interim Guidelines, Section 6.C.1, likewise require a minimum of 8.23 maf to be released from Glen Canyon Dam each year, except for reductions specified by the Interim Guidelines. The 2008 Final Biological Opinion describes this 8.23 maf figure as Reclamation's baseline minimum objective annual release, with the proposed action allowing releases below it only under conditions defined in the Shortage Guidelines. As of the 2025 Post-2026 Alternatives Report, Reclamation affirms that under LROC Article II(2) the objective remains a minimum release of 8.23 maf, and plans to publish any annual deficits below that objective release alongside 10-year Lee Ferry aggregate flow metrics.

The 2007 Interim Guidelines were developed to improve management of Colorado River water supplies and to provide water users a greater degree of predictability/certainty regarding the timing and volume of annual water deliveries and potential delivery reductions, particularly under drought and low-reservoir conditions.

The 2007 Interim Guidelines are implemented annually by the Secretary through the Criteria for Coordinated Long-Range Operation of Colorado River Reservoirs (LROC), established pursuant to the Colorado River Basin Project Act (CRBPA) of September 30, 1968, and issued via the Annual Operating Plan (AOP). The AOP itself is the single, integrated reference document required by Section 602(b) of the CRBPA of 1968, and it memorializes operational decisions made under multiple individual federal actions, including the Interim Surplus Guidelines, the 1996 Glen Canyon Dam ROD, and the 2007 Interim Guidelines.

Under the Upper Basin DCP's DROA, Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above elevation 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool (EU-LP-CRS-001-04). Reclamation's stated operational goal under DROA is to 'protect' this 3,525-ft elevation, primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial-unit reservoirs (EU-LP-CRS-002-04). The DROA establishes the process for Reclamation, in collaboration with the Upper Basin States, to release additional water from upstream CRSP initial-unit reservoirs (Flaming Gorge, Aspinall, Navajo, Glen Canyon/Lake Powell) to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation (EU-LP-OFF-017-03). In CRSS modeling, Powell Infrastructure Protection (PIP) releases from the Upper Initial Units (Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Navajo) are specifically triggered when Lake Powell is projected to fall below elevation 3,525 feet (EU-LP-OFF-021-06). This target was actually invoked when the July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell declining below the 3,525.00-ft DROA target elevation, triggering DROA year-2025 drought-response planning under the DCP-related agreements (EU-LP-OFF-022-03); consistent with protecting this same target, the December 2025 24-Month Study reduced Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes for December 2025 through April 2026 by 0.598 maf (EU-LP-OFF-023-03).

Under the 2024 near-term consensus agreement / 2024 ROD's new Section XI.G.6.E (per CRS summary and the official Record of Decision), if the minimum probable 24-Month Study projects an elevation below 3,500 feet at Lake Powell in the next 12 months, the Secretary must begin planning to reduce Lake Powell releases as needed to not less than 6.0 maf for the Water Year to maintain elevation 3,500 feet -- in lieu of a 7.0 maf figure referenced under the near-term proposal framing.

The 2007 Interim Guidelines were deliberately designed as a 20-year 'interim' framework and are scheduled to expire at the end of 2026, alongside other Colorado River operating instruments (the 2019 Drought Contingency Plans and international Minutes 323/330). This 2026 expiration is the trigger for Reclamation's post-2026 operations review: DOI formally initiated the Post-2026 NEPA process on June 16, 2023 to develop successor operating guidelines for Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam effective when the 2007 Interim Guidelines expire, and Basin States were subsequently asked to submit a preliminary post-2026 agreement by mid-November 2025 and a final seven-state agreement by mid-February 2026, targeting implementation for the 2027 operating year.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The DROA states that drought response operations 'will not extend beyond' the 2007 ROD term (December 31, 2025, after finalization of the 2026 AOP), while the July 2026 24-Month Study describes a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan and Reclamation states the DCPs expire at the end of 2026; the evidence set does not explain how the 2026 DROA actions relate to that term clause. The successor guidelines were not adopted in the evidence set.
items.operational_implication: Any rule cited for Lake Powell's annual release needs its instrument and expiration date; after 2026 the governing framework depends on which post-2026 alternative is adopted.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-001 confirmed the storage decline 'from 55.8 maf (approximately 94 percent of capacity) to 32.1 maf (approximately 54 percent of capacity)' as background to the 2007 decision. OFF-002 confirmed 'The decision is to adjust the 2007 Interim Guidelines'. items.title: September 2005: low reservoir elevation let oxygen-depleted water through the penstocks
items.operational_question: What caused the September 2005 drop in dissolved oxygen below Glen Canyon Dam, and how was it addressed operationally?
items.synthesis_claim: In fall 2005, dissolved oxygen in the river below Glen Canyon Dam fell below 4.0 mg/L, the 1-day mean minimum used for the cold-water fishery. Sources document the mechanism: an oxygen-depleted plume formed in the metalimnion, and because Lake Powell was at its lowest level in decades (3,555 ft in April 2005), that layer sat just above the 3,470 ft penstock intakes and was withdrawn through the dam. In most years the metalimnion is high enough above the penstocks that this does not happen. The operational response was to run more turbines at lower flows and lower efficiency, which tests showed increased aeration.
items.scope_and_conditions: A single episode in summer-fall 2005 at Glen Canyon Dam. The 4.0 / 5.0 / 6.5 mg/L values are the 1-day, 7-day, and 30-day mean minimum criteria cited for cold-water fish in RES-020. The 'lowest since initial filling' wording in RES-020 and 'lowest since 1969' in RES-019 refer to the same 2005 low.

analysis_chain.statement: In most years the metalimnetic oxygen minimum does not affect releases because it lies well above the penstock elevation of 3,470 ft; release temperature and quality depend on which reservoir layer is at the intake.
Lake Powell fell to 3,555.02 ft on April 8, 2005, its lowest level since 1969.

An oxygen-depleted plume extending to the dam was captured in the penstock withdrawal zone and exported downstream; river DO dropped below 4.0 mg/L in September 2005, a concern for the cold-water fishery given its 1-day 4.0 mg/L minimum.
Turbine aeration tests found that running turbines at lower flows and lower generating efficiencies increased aeration most, and more turbines were then operated at lower flows to raise DO.

supporting_evidence.summary: In most years the metalimnetic oxygen minimum does not affect dam discharges because it sits well above the penstock elevation (3,470 ft), but in 2005 reservoir elevations were the lowest since initial filling and the low-DO metalimnetic water was located just above the penstock elevation, allowing oxygen-depleted water to pass through the dam.

supporting_evidence.summary: In fall 2005, a plume of oxygen-depleted water in Lake Powell was captured in the penstock withdrawal zone and exported through Glen Canyon Dam, dropping tailwater dissolved oxygen below 4.0 mg/L in September 2005 and violating EPA cold-water fishery DO criteria (1-day mean minimum 4.0 mg/L, 7-day mean minimum 5.0 mg/L, 30-day mean 6.5 mg/L) (RES-020-02). This occurred because in most years the metalimnetic oxygen minimum sits well above the penstock elevation (3,470 ft) and does not affect dam discharges, but in 2005 reservoir elevations were the lowest since initial filling, placing the low-DO metalimnetic layer just above the penstock elevation and allowing oxygen-depleted water to pass through the dam (RES-020-07).

The DO criteria are cited as requirements for cold-water fish species in a modeling report, not as a dam operating rule.
items.operational_implication: Low storage can impair release water quality as well as quantity; drawdown toward the penstock elevation increases the chance that poor-quality reservoir layers reach the intakes.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading RES-020 confirmed the mechanism ('This water was captured in the withdrawal zone of the release intakes (penstocks) and exported through the dam') and the criteria ('requirements of a 1-day mean minimum concentration of 4.0 mg/L, a 7-day mean minimum of 5.0 mg/L, and a 30-day mean of 6.5 mg/L for cold water fish species'). The corrective action was confirmed as 'more turbines were operated at lower flows to increase DO concentrations'.

items.title: The 1997 and 2000 sediment flows failed to build sandbars, and HFEs were later tied to tributary sand inputs
items.operational_question: Why did the 1997 Test Flow and the 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow experiment fail to build sandbars, and how did HFE practice change afterwards?
items.synthesis_claim: Two early experimental releases intended to build sandbars did not achieve that target, for different documented reasons. The November 1997 Test Flow followed a period of high releases that had already transported much of the available sand, and its magnitude was judged insufficient to deposit sand at higher elevations. The 2000 experiment's two high flows produced minimal sandbar building because the Paria River had supplied very little sediment beforehand, and the reduced summer hydrograph was followed by tamarisk seedling proliferation on bare sand. Following study of early HFEs, Reclamation developed a formal 2011 protocol, and from 2012 HFEs were timed to follow large tributary sand inputs.
items.scope_and_conditions: Experimental releases at Glen Canyon Dam in 1997 and 2000 as analyzed by USGS (RES-018) and summarized in the LTEMP FEIS. The link between these specific failures and the later protocol is stated generally in the sources ('following study of the early HFEs'); the sources do not attribute the protocol to these two experiments alone.

analysis_chain.statement: The 1997 Test Flow was Reclamation's first attempt at a post-tributary-flood sediment-redistribution release; the 2000 experiment included two high flows intended to build sandbars.

The 1997 Test Flow did not significantly aggrade sandbars; it came during a period of high releases with high sediment transport that reduced available sediment, and its magnitude was not sufficient to distribute sand to higher depositional locations.

Minimal sandbar building occurred during either high flow in 2000 because the Paria River supplied very little sediment in prior months; the reduced summer hydrograph was followed by proliferation of tamarisk seedlings on bare sand.

After study of the early HFEs, Reclamation developed a 2011 HFE protocol setting conditions and a method for timing, magnitude, and duration, and since 2012 HFEs follow a decision protocol timed to large tributary sand inputs.

supporting_evidence.summary: The November 3, 1997 Test Flow (a constant 872 m3/s release for 48 hours), the first Reclamation attempt at a post-tributary-flood sediment-redistribution release, did not significantly aggrade sandbars because its magnitude was insufficient to distribute sand to open depositional locations at higher elevations.

supporting_evidence.summary: Two early post-dam sediment-redistribution flow experiments, predating the LTEMP HFE protocol, failed to achieve their sandbar-building objectives, each for a different reason. The November 3, 1997 Test Flow (a constant 872 m3/s release for 48 hours), Reclamation's first attempt at a post-tributary-flood sediment-redistribution release, did not significantly aggrade sandbars because its magnitude was insufficient to distribute sand to open depositional locations at higher elevations (RES-018-09). The 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow Experiment (a 4-day 864 m3/s release, 3 months of constant 227 m3/s, then a 4-day 881 m3/s release) produced minimal sandbar building because the Paria River had supplied very little sediment beforehand, and the sustained low, steady discharge instead allowed proliferation of invasive tamarisk seedlings on bare sand deposits (RES-018-10).

High flow experiments were tested in 1996, 1997, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2013, and 2014 to rebuild eroded sandbars; since 2012 a 10-year protocol implements one to two high flow experiments annually, timed to follow tributary sand inputs from the Paria River in fall and/or spring (EU-LP-RES-014-05). This decision-making protocol, approved by the Department of the Interior in 2012, coordinates dam releases to occur following large sand inputs delivered to the Colorado River by a major tributary (EU-LP-RES-018-01). Across the full historical record, 11 HFEs were released from Glen Canyon Dam between 1996 and November 2018, with peak magnitudes ranging from 864 to 1,274 cubic meters per second and durations from 24 to 168 hours, including lower-magnitude habitat maintenance flows (HMFs) in 1997 and 2000 (EU-LP-RES-018-02).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: Causes are those reported by the USGS synthesis (citing Hazel and others, 2000, and Schmidt and others, 2007); the evidence set does not include the original experiment reports. The 1996 controlled flood is treated in the sources as a separate, more successful test and is not part of this failure episode.

items.title: The 1965 tailrace slab failure during outlet-works operation at 3,490 ft informs today's reliance limits
items.operational_question: What happened when Glen Canyon Dam's river outlet works were operated at minimum power pool in 1965, and how does that episode bear on current low-elevation operations?
items.synthesis_claim: On the night of April 20, 1965, with the reservoir at 3,490 ft, four of eight units running, and three outlets partly or mostly open, the tailrace slab was undermined and partly collapsed. Reclamation's 2024 technical memorandum attributes this to a recirculating eddy that was stronger than in the 1964 physical model because the outlets were operated at low head, with fewer units and lower tailwater than modeled. The outlet works have otherwise been used only briefly, at elevations well above 3,490 ft, and the design record does not indicate they were intended for long-term conveyance at low levels. Together with tailrace scour concerns, these findings support Reclamation's 2024 recommendation not to rely on the outlet works as the sole release path below minimum power pool.
items.scope_and_conditions: Glen Canyon Dam river outlet works and tailrace, 1965 to the March 2024 Interim Operating Guidance. A 2023 cavitation report comes from a media source and is not treated here as a documented failure; the 2024 memorandum states that 2023 outlet releases were made at levels well above 3,490 ft.

analysis_chain.statement: On April 20, 1965, the tailrace slab was undermined and portions sank, with the reservoir at 3,490 ft, four of eight units operating, Outlet 1 closed, Outlet 2 25% open, Outlets 3 and 4 90% open, and tailwater 4-6 ft lower than predicted in model studies.

Reclamation's memorandum states that operating the outlets at 3,490 ft rather than the 3,700 ft used in the model, with fewer units and lower tailwater, intensified a recirculating eddy whose reverse flow scoured and undermined the slab.

The outlet works were used when the dam first filled, during short high-flow experiments, and for early-1980s flood releases, but never over extended periods; the design references give no indication they were intended for long-term conveyance at low reservoir levels.

Citing uncertainty about long-term performance of the conduits and components and about tailrace scour and sediment deposition, Reclamation recommended in 2024 not relying on the outlet works as the sole release means below 3,490 ft.

supporting_evidence.summary: On April 20, 1965, while the reservoir was at elevation 3,490 ft with four of eight powerplant units operating and outlets variably open, the Glen Canyon Dam tailrace stabilization slab was undermined by a recirculating eddy from river outlet works operation and portions of it collapsed, because tailwater was 4-6 feet lower than predicted by physical modeling.

supporting_evidence.summary: Multiple sources indicate the river outlet works (ROW) were not designed for, and cannot be fully relied upon for, long-term or high-flow releases at low Lake Powell levels. Reclamation's 2024 Technical Decision Memorandum found no design reference indicating the ROW were intended for long-term water conveyance at low reservoir levels; historically they were used only to augment powerplant/spillway discharges for short durations (e.g., about three months during 1983 flood releases, days to a week for high-flow experiments) (OFF-025-04). A 2023 special inspection found the hollow-jet valves, pipes, and ring-follower gates sufficient for periodic/seasonal releases but flagged concern about long-term high-flow use and recommended a major overhaul or replacement for high confidence in continuous long-term operation (OFF-025-05). This concern has historical precedent: on April 20, 1965, at reservoir elevation 3,490 ft with the ROW variably open, the dam's tailrace stabilization slab was undermined by a recirculating eddy from ROW operation and portions of it collapsed, because tailwater was 4-6 feet lower than had been predicted by physical modeling (OFF-025-06). More recently, in 2023, when the ROW were used for a high-flow release into the Grand Canyon at low-reservoir levels, damaging cavitation occurred, and the Bureau has warned further extended use would likely cause more (MED-002-03). Based on this evidence, Reclamation's formal conclusion is that it should not rely on the ROW as the sole means of releasing water from Glen Canyon Dam, as would be required below minimum power pool (3,490 ft), given current uncertainty about long-term conduit and hollow-jet valve performance and tailrace sedimentation (OFF-025-07).

The River Outlet Works (bypass tubes) have historically only been opened when the dam was first filled, during short-term high-flow experiments, and for emergency flood releases in the early 1980s, and have never been used over extended periods (EU-LP-CRS-002-03). Below minimum power pool, the River Outlet Works are the only remaining way to pass water through Glen Canyon Dam: two intakes leading to four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes with a combined maximum discharge capacity of 15,000 cubic feet per second (EU-LP-MED-002-02), a capacity figure confirmed on Reclamation's own project page, which also lists a combined spillway discharge capacity of 208,000 cfs at elevation 3,700.0 ft (EU-LP-OFF-030-02). Since the Draft SEIS, Reclamation identified enhanced risks associated with relying on the River Outlet Works as the exclusive means of releasing water at low reservoir elevations for sustained periods, prompting the 2024 Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels (EU-LP-OFF-007-04).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The evidence does not describe how the 1965 slab was repaired or whether the tailrace was redesigned. The 2023 cavitation statement (MED-002) is not corroborated by an official source in this evidence set.
items.operational_implication: The only documented case of outlet-works operation at minimum power pool involved structural damage, so the outlet works cannot be treated as a proven substitute for the penstocks at low elevations.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading OFF-025 Section D.5 confirmed the conditions at failure and the cause: 'Operating the river outlets at reservoir elevation 3,490 instead of at normal water surface elevation 3,700 ft as used in the model, caused the jets to impinge closer to the weir' and 'The scour from the reverse flow undermined the toe of the slab and rapidly removed its foundation, causing collapse of the slab.' Section D.2 confirmed later outlet releases 'were made at reservoir levels well above elevation 3,490 ft'. The candidate card's inclusion of 2023 cavitation as a second failure episode was dropped because only a media source reports it.

items.title: Lake Powell fell below the 3,525 ft DROA target in 2023 and again in 2026 despite drought-response actions
items.operational_question: Has the DROA target elevation of 3,525 ft been maintained since drought response operations began in 2021?
items.synthesis_claim: The DROA target of 3,525 ft, set as a 35 ft buffer above minimum power pool, has not been maintained. Drought response actions began in 2021 with upstream releases (161,000 af per the DROA page; 180,000 af per CRS) and continued in 2022 with reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and a Flaming Gorge transfer, yet Lake Powell storage fell in 2021 and 2022 and the reservoir reached 3,520 ft on March 11, 2023, its lowest recorded level and below the target. The target was projected to be breached again in 2025, and on July 26, 2026 the reservoir stood at 3,522.90 ft with an end-of-2026 projection of 3,507.68 ft, despite the 2026 Section 6.E release reduction and DROA releases.
items.scope_and_conditions: Lake Powell elevations and DROA actions from summer 2021 to July 2026. The 3,525 ft target is a risk-management target, not a regulatory requirement; reaching an elevation below it is an unmet target, not a breach of law. Upstream release volumes for 2021 differ between sources (see KC-LP-EMR-05).

analysis_chain.statement: DROA defines 3,525 ft as the target elevation for minimizing the risk of falling below 3,490 ft, providing a 35 ft buffer for response actions.

Beginning in summer 2021 Reclamation released water from upstream initial units to protect the target elevation (161,000 af per the DROA page; 180,000 af from Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, and Navajo per CRS), and in 2022 reduced Lake Powell releases from 7.48 to 7.00 maf.

Lake Powell and Lake Mead ended water year 2022 at their lowest levels since initial filling; Lake Powell storage fell in 2021 and 2022 despite the DROA changes, and on March 11, 2023 the reservoir reached 3,520 ft, its lowest on record and below the 3,525 ft target.

The July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell below the 3,525 ft target, triggering drought-response planning; on July 26, 2026 the reservoir was at 3,522.90 ft with a projected end-of-calendar-year elevation of 3,507.68 ft.
The 2000-2022 period was the driest 23-year period in more than a century in the Colorado River Basin.

supporting_evidence.summary: The Drought Response Operations Agreement (DROA) defines elevation 3,525 ft as the 'target elevation' at Lake Powell for minimizing the risk of the reservoir declining below 3,490 ft, providing a 35-foot buffer above minimum power pool to allow response actions before Lake Powell drops below 3,490 ft.

supporting_evidence.summary: Under the Upper Basin DCP's DROA, Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above elevation 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool (EU-LP-CRS-001-04). Reclamation's stated operational goal under DROA is to 'protect' this 3,525-ft elevation, primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial-unit reservoirs (EU-LP-CRS-002-04). The DROA establishes the process for Reclamation, in collaboration with the Upper Basin States, to release additional water from upstream CRSP initial-unit reservoirs (Flaming Gorge, Aspinall, Navajo, Glen Canyon/Lake Powell) to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation (EU-LP-OFF-017-03). In CRSS modeling, Powell Infrastructure Protection (PIP) releases from the Upper Initial Units (Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Navajo) are specifically triggered when Lake Powell is projected to fall below elevation 3,525 feet (EU-LP-OFF-021-06). This target was actually invoked when the July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell declining below the 3,525.00-ft DROA target elevation, triggering DROA year-2025 drought-response planning under the DCP-related agreements (EU-LP-OFF-022-03); consistent with protecting this same target, the December 2025 24-Month Study reduced Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes for December 2025 through April 2026 by 0.598 maf (EU-LP-OFF-023-03).

CRS R47497 states that in 2021 Reclamation transferred 180,000 acre-feet to Lake Powell from Flaming Gorge (125,000 AF), Blue Mesa (36,000 AF), and Navajo (20,000 AF) reservoirs, and in 2022 reduced Lake Powell releases from 7.48 to 7.00 maf while transferring an additional 0.50 maf from Flaming Gorge (EU-LP-CRS-002-05). Reclamation's own DROA program page states that beginning summer 2021, pursuant to the DROA, Reclamation determined an imminent need to release 161,000 acre-feet from the upstream Flaming Gorge and Aspinall Unit (Blue Mesa) Initial Units, and that in January 2022 it additionally modified Glen Canyon Dam releases, readjusting 350,000 acre-feet, to protect critical elevations at Lake Powell (EU-LP-OFF-031-03). The two sources give different acre-foot totals for what appears to be overlapping 2021-2022 DROA-triggered actions (180,000 AF vs. 161,000 AF for 2021; a 0.50 maf Flaming Gorge transfer vs. a 350,000 AF Glen Canyon Dam release readjustment for 2022), and neither source alone clarifies whether these figures represent the same actions counted differently, partial vs. final tallies, or genuinely distinct actions.

Two independent Reclamation documents state the identical drought-severity statistic: the period from 2000 through 2022 was the driest/lowest 23-year period in more than a century of record and one of the driest/lowest such periods in the last 1,200 years in the Colorado River Basin. The 2024 Near-term Colorado River Operations SEIS Record of Decision cites this as the basis for supplementing the 2007 Interim Guidelines (OFF-002-07), and the Draft 2026 Annual Operating Plan restates the same statistic while separately reporting that total system storage fell by 3.37 MAF during water year 2025, from 43 percent to 37 percent of capacity (OFF-022-07).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The sources do not attribute the shortfall to any specific cause or quantify how much lower the reservoir would have been without DROA actions, so the effectiveness of the actions cannot be assessed here. The 2021 upstream release volume is reported as both 161,000 af and 180,000 af. The 2026 end-of-year elevation is a projection.
items.operational_implication: The 35 ft buffer above minimum power pool has been partly consumed twice within five years, so the target should be read as a trigger for action rather than as an elevation that operations can reliably hold.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading CRS-002 confirmed: 'Lake Powell storage levels fell in 2021 and 2022, despite the most recent changes under DROA. Lake Powell's March 11, 2023, elevation of 3,520 fasl was the lake's lowest level on record ... below Reclamation's target protection volume of 3,525 fasl.' OFF-024 confirmed the July 26, 2026 elevation of 3,522.90 ft and the projected EOCY 2026 elevation of 3,507.68 ft. OFF-031 confirmed the 161,000 af figure 'to protect the target elevation'. The candidate claim was kept descriptive; no causal attribution is made for the shortfall.

items.title: Even with the 2026 drought-response package, Lake Powell is projected to fall to within 2 ft of minimum power pool in spring 2027
items.operational_question: What Lake Powell elevations does Reclamation project after the 2026 release reduction and Flaming Gorge releases, compared with the elevation thresholds those actions are meant to protect?
items.synthesis_claim: The 2026 actions change the projected trajectory but do not keep Lake Powell above all protective thresholds. Without major intervention, the April 2026 24-Month Study projected a decline below 3,490 ft by August 2026. The July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study, which includes the 6.00 maf WY2026 release, keeps the reservoir above 3,500 ft through January 2027 but projects it below 3,500 ft from February to April 2027, reaching 3,491.75 ft in April 2027, only 1.75 ft above minimum power pool, before spring runoff raises it to about 3,524 ft by June-July 2027. That trajectory stays below the 3,525 ft DROA target for the whole projection period shown.
items.scope_and_conditions: Projection from a single model run (July 2026 24-Month Study, Most Probable inflow scenario, Model Run ID 3322) with a modeled WY2026 release of 6.00 maf and WY2027 release of 7.00 maf. Projections under minimum probable inflow, which would be lower, are not in the evidence set. This is a projection, not an observed outcome.

analysis_chain.statement: Interior reduced the WY2026 Lake Powell release from 7.48 to 6.00 maf under Section 6.E, paired with DROA releases of about 0.66-1.0 maf from Flaming Gorge by April 2027.
Reclamation's April 2026 24-Month Study projected that Lake Powell may decline below 3,490 ft by August 2026 without major intervention.

The July 2026 Most Probable run shows Lake Powell at 3,522.28 ft at the end of July 2026, declining to a low of 3,491.75 ft in April 2027 before rising to about 3,524 ft in July 2027; the July 26, 2026 weekly update gives a projected end-of-2026 elevation of 3,507.68 ft.
Section 6.E aims to maintain 3,500 ft and the DROA target is 3,525 ft; the projected trajectory is below 3,525 ft throughout and below 3,500 ft from February to April 2027.

supporting_evidence.summary: Because historically dry WY2026 conditions caused Lake Powell to be projected to decline below elevation 3,500 feet, the Department of the Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to reduce Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, coupled with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing approximately 660,000 to 1.00 maf of additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to Lake Powell by April 2027.

supporting_evidence.summary: On April 17, 2026, the Bureau of Reclamation announced unprecedented actions to store more water in Lake Powell -- then less than 25 percent full -- to preserve hydropower generation and protect Glen Canyon Dam water-delivery infrastructure the agency said was at risk from low reservoir levels (EU-LP-MED-001-01). With the consent of the four Upper Basin states, Reclamation committed to releasing between 660,000 and 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (82 percent full) into Lake Powell over the 12 months following the announcement, building on a smaller 463,000-acre-foot release used to prop up Powell in 2022-23 (EU-LP-MED-001-02). Because WY2026 was historically dry and Lake Powell was projected to decline below elevation 3,500 feet, the Department of the Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to reduce Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, coupled with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing approximately 660,000 to 1.00 maf of additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to Lake Powell by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-023-02). Reclamation's newsroom release confirms the combined plan: adding about 2.48 million acre-feet via the 660,000 AF-1 maf Flaming Gorge release (April 2026-April 2027, under the 2019 Drought Response Operating Agreements) plus the 7.48-to-6.0-maf release reduction through September 2026 under Section 6E, together expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation about 54 feet to at least 3,500 feet by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-035-02).

Under the 2024 near-term consensus agreement / 2024 ROD's new Section XI.G.6.E (per CRS summary and the official Record of Decision), if the minimum probable 24-Month Study projects an elevation below 3,500 feet at Lake Powell in the next 12 months, the Secretary must begin planning to reduce Lake Powell releases as needed to not less than 6.0 maf for the Water Year to maintain elevation 3,500 feet -- in lieu of a 7.0 maf figure referenced under the near-term proposal framing.

Under the Upper Basin DCP's DROA, Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above elevation 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool (EU-LP-CRS-001-04). Reclamation's stated operational goal under DROA is to 'protect' this 3,525-ft elevation, primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial-unit reservoirs (EU-LP-CRS-002-04). The DROA establishes the process for Reclamation, in collaboration with the Upper Basin States, to release additional water from upstream CRSP initial-unit reservoirs (Flaming Gorge, Aspinall, Navajo, Glen Canyon/Lake Powell) to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation (EU-LP-OFF-017-03). In CRSS modeling, Powell Infrastructure Protection (PIP) releases from the Upper Initial Units (Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Navajo) are specifically triggered when Lake Powell is projected to fall below elevation 3,525 feet (EU-LP-OFF-021-06). This target was actually invoked when the July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell declining below the 3,525.00-ft DROA target elevation, triggering DROA year-2025 drought-response planning under the DCP-related agreements (EU-LP-OFF-022-03); consistent with protecting this same target, the December 2025 24-Month Study reduced Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes for December 2025 through April 2026 by 0.598 maf (EU-LP-OFF-023-03).

Reclamation's original Technical Record of Design and Construction established elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum reservoir elevation for power production, 20 ft above the penstock intake centerline (elevation 3,470 ft); water cannot be released through the penstocks below 3,490 ft (OFF-025-03). Multiple later sources restate this same threshold: Reclamation estimates the depth for minimum power pool is 20 ft above the penstocks, i.e. elevation 3,490 fasl (CRS-002-02); at 3,490 ft, minimum power pool is 20 ft above the generators' actual penstock intakes, and the dam's eight turbines must be shut down at minimum power pool to avoid cavitation (MED-002-01); the 1999 multi-level intake structure hydraulic model study likewise designates elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum water surface for power operations (OFF-028-06); the 2016 LTEMP Final EIS states hydropower production would cease if Lake Powell drops below approximately 3,490 ft (OFF-005-01); the 2024 Near-term Operations SEIS ROD notes dry hydrology in recent years produced low Lake Powell elevations at levels such as 3,490 ft, giving Reclamation operating experience at this threshold (OFF-002-06); the 2024 LTEMP Final Supplemental EIS states Reclamation's Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels directs use of the full extent of Upper Colorado Basin operational capabilities to try to keep Lake Powell at or above elevation 3,490 ft (OFF-007-03); and an April 2026 status report reiterates that hydropower generation stops at 3,490 feet, with the reservoir at 3,526 feet at that time and Reclamation aiming to keep it above 3,500 feet (MED-001-04).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The two projections use different study months (April vs. July 2026) and possibly different inflow scenarios, so the difference between them is not a clean measure of the effect of the actions. The projection depends on WY2027 inflow (modeled at 7.25 maf unregulated) and on an assumed 7.00 maf WY2027 release; further Section 6.E reductions in WY2027 are not modeled in this run.
items.operational_implication: The 2026 package buys time rather than restoring the buffer: under the most probable inflow the reservoir is still projected to come close to minimum power pool before the 2027 runoff, so further action in WY2027 may be needed.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading the OFF-023 Lake Powell table confirmed the end-of-month elevations: 'Jul 2026 ... 3522.28', 'Dec 2026 ... 3507.68', 'Jan 2027 ... 3501.25', 'Feb 2027 ... 3496.16', 'Mar 2027 ... 3491.92', 'Apr 2027 ... 3491.75', 'Jun 2027 ... 3524.59', 'Jul 2027 ... 3524.13', with WY2026 total release 6000 and WY2027 total release 7000 (kaf). The EU-LP-OFF-023-06 quote is only the table header; the elevations were verified directly in the table. Confidence was set to medium because this is a single projection run.

items.title: Frequent HFEs increased sand volume at most monitoring sites, but not at every bar type, and campsite area still declined
items.operational_question: What sandbar and campsite outcomes have been observed downstream of Glen Canyon Dam during the period of frequent HFEs?
items.synthesis_claim: Against a background of net sand erosion in most post-dam years, the period of frequent controlled floods was followed by net sand deposition at most monitoring sites: from 2004 to 2020, with seven HFEs and above-average tributary sand input in more than half of the years, 86% of long-term sites gained sand. The response differs by bar type: wide reattachment bars and upper pool deposits have stabilized under vegetation and reached their maximum size, while separation bars and undifferentiated eddy bars aggrade during HFEs but have continued to decline over time. Over 2002-2016, usable campsite area at the same sites fell 37%, with vegetation encroachment the primary cause, so sand gains have not translated into recreational campsite area.
items.scope_and_conditions: Observed outcomes at the 45 long-term sandbar monitoring sites in Marble and Grand Canyons, mostly 1990-2020, as reported by USGS and the LTEMP EIS. The 2004-2020 result reflects HFEs together with tributary sand supply and other flow conditions; the sources do not attribute the gains to HFEs alone.

analysis_chain.statement: The dam cut off about 95% of the historical sediment supply, and from 1964 to 2017 net sand erosion occurred in about 69% of years in Marble Canyon and 52% in Grand Canyon.
Since 2012 HFEs have followed a protocol timed to tributary sand inputs; sandbars were larger at 52%, 52%, and 57% of monitoring sites immediately after the 2012, 2013, and 2014 HFEs.
From 2004 to 2020, a period with seven controlled floods and above-average tributary sand input in more than half the years, net deposition occurred at 86% of long-term monitoring sites.

At vegetated, stage-limited bar types HFEs can do no better than replace sediment eroded between events as accommodation space diminishes, while HFEs have not changed the long-term declining trajectory of undifferentiated eddy bars and separation bars.
From 2002 to 2016 usable campsite area declined 37% at the same sites, with vegetation encroachment identified as the primary cause.

supporting_evidence.summary: Glen Canyon Dam cut off approximately 95 percent of the historical sediment supply from the upper watershed, and from 1964 to 2017 this resulted in net sand erosion in about 69 percent of years in Marble Canyon and about 52 percent of years in Grand Canyon.

supporting_evidence.summary: Glen Canyon Dam's High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol effectiveness is tracked through a network of 45 long-term sandbar monitoring sites, part of a larger repeat topographic/bathymetric survey program (approximately 1,800 surveys) that represents only 7-9 percent of all sandbars in Marble and Grand Canyons but has been shown, by comparison with larger samples, to consistently characterize system-wide average sandbar response. At these 45 sites, sandbars were measured as larger at 52%, 52%, and 57% of sites immediately following the 2012, 2013, and 2014 HFEs respectively, with total sand volume at these sites increasing over the program's first 4 years. For the five HFEs released between 2012 and 2018, pre/post-event topographic surveys were not conducted; instead sandbar response was assessed via daily repeat photographs from remote automated cameras plus annual monitoring surveys collected approximately 11 months after each event.

The long-term effectiveness of the High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol at rebuilding Grand Canyon sandbars differs by bar type and has structural limits at both ends. At wide reattachment bars and upper pool deposits, vegetation stabilization and vertical aggradation during successive HFEs have progressively narrowed the channel and reduced the accommodation space available for further deposition, so at best HFEs can only replace sediment eroded during normal dam operations between events rather than produce net growth (RES-018-12). At separation bars and undifferentiated eddy bars, HFEs have not effectively rebuilt the bars, which have continued to gradually decrease in volume over time; although these bars consistently aggrade during individual HFEs, the subsequent erosion at these unvegetated, wind-exposed sites is rapid (RES-018-13).

High flow experiments were tested in 1996, 1997, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2013, and 2014 to rebuild eroded sandbars; since 2012 a 10-year protocol implements one to two high flow experiments annually, timed to follow tributary sand inputs from the Paria River in fall and/or spring (EU-LP-RES-014-05). This decision-making protocol, approved by the Department of the Interior in 2012, coordinates dam releases to occur following large sand inputs delivered to the Colorado River by a major tributary (EU-LP-RES-018-01). Across the full historical record, 11 HFEs were released from Glen Canyon Dam between 1996 and November 2018, with peak magnitudes ranging from 864 to 1,274 cubic meters per second and durations from 24 to 168 hours, including lower-magnitude habitat maintenance flows (HMFs) in 1997 and 2000 (EU-LP-RES-018-02).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The observed gains coincide with above-average tributary sand input, so the sources do not isolate the HFE contribution. Monitoring sites are a sample of the river corridor. Campsite data cover 2002-2016 and sandbar data extend to 2020, so the periods differ.
items.operational_implication: HFE performance should be judged by bar type and by campsite area, not only by total sand volume, because the same flows can increase sand while vegetation reduces usable area.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading RES-018 confirmed 'In the period from 2004 to 2020, which included seven controlled floods ... and greater than average tributary sand inputs in more than half of the years, net deposition occurred at 86 percent of long-term monitoring sites', that 'HFEs have not been effective at changing the long-term trajectory of undifferentiated eddy bars and separation bars', and that campsite area 'declined by 37 percent ... and that vegetation encroachment was the primary cause'. OFF-007 confirmed the 95% sediment cutoff and the 69% / 52% erosion-year shares. The claim avoids attributing the 2004-2020 gains to HFEs alone.
